#9708. I Built a Tool That Lets You Work on Multiple Projects in One AI Environment

Use separate MCP endpoints to give each project its own services, then switch access without rebuilding your setup.

An online store has an order-status bug. A booking service has an availability problem. You want an AI assistant to investigate both, in separate conversations, while you review the results in the same development environment.

Opening another chat is easy. Keeping the tools attached to each project understandable takes more care. Both projects might use PostgreSQL and Redis. Both might have tables called users. A tool named “query database” says very little about which application it can reach.

The setup in this walkthrough gives each project a named access path: one MCP endpoint for the store, another for the booking service. Both can stay available while work runs in parallel. Each also has a switch for temporarily stopping access, without deleting its configuration.

Disclosure: I build GateRook, the application used below. The screenshots show a local development build with fictional project data.

There are two things to organize when working on several projects with AI.

The first is the working context: the repository, instructions, conversation history, and task. Give each project its own workspace and conversation in your AI application.

The second is access to external services. The store needs its orders database and cache. The booking service needs its reservations database and availability cache. These are different resources even when they use the same technology.

MCP provides the connection between an AI application and tools. Its architecture allows a host application to connect to multiple servers; it does not prescribe how that application manages the model's context. That distinction matters here. MCP architecture overview

In GateRook, an endpoint is one MCP URL with its own selected connections, tool modes, and tokens. For this example, the layout is:

The same AI application can be configured with both endpoint URLs. Calls through shop-dev use the store's configured services; calls through booking-dev use the booking service's configured services.

That does not automatically bind a particular chat to an endpoint. If an AI client exposes both endpoints globally, both may be available in either conversation. Use its project-level configuration when you need project-specific tool availability.

Start by creating two endpoints in GateRook: shop-dev and booking-dev. Use names that identify the project and environment before any tool call happens.

Create the database and cache connections for each project. In the connection wizard's endpoint step, add shop-db and shop-cache only to shop-dev. Add booking-db and booking-cache only to booking-dev.

Then open Overview and select each endpoint. This is a useful check: does the list of services match the project you think you are working on?

Keep the underlying credentials scoped too. The two demo database connections use separate PostgreSQL roles with read access to their respective project tables. GateRook's connection test reported SELECT access and no table ownership or CREATE privilege.

This matters because an endpoint's tool policy and a database role govern different parts of a request. An approval in the gateway cannot grant a database privilege the role does not have. PostgreSQL documents these permissions separately, including SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE. PostgreSQL privileges

For an investigation, enable the reads you need and review the write-capable tools. You can leave mutations behind approval or turn them off for that endpoint. Avoid giving a debugging session an administrator account just because it is convenient to configure.

From Overview, select shop-dev, choose Connect an AI app, and follow the setup for your client. Review the configuration change before saving it. Repeat from booking-dev for the same client.

For the local Cursor example, this produces two server entries, gaterook-shop-dev and gaterook-booking-dev, pointing to different endpoint URLs. Complete any enable or restart step requested by the client before using the tools.

Choose the configuration scope deliberately. Cursor supports project configuration in .cursor/mcp.json and global configuration in ~/.cursor/mcp.json. Global entries are available across projects, so adding two global entries is a convenient shared setup, not a per-project access restriction. For project-specific availability, configure only the appropriate endpoint in each workspace and remove any global duplicate that exposes the other project. Keep literal tokens out of committed configuration. Cursor MCP documentation

The screenshots show configured access in GateRook. The connection map is not a display of live agent traffic.

With both endpoints enabled, keep a store conversation and a booking conversation open. Each should identify the project, the allowed endpoint, and the expected result.

Work on the online store. Use the shop-dev endpoint and shop-db connection. Read the orders schema and summarize order counts by status. Do not change data. Include the connection name in your result.

Work on the booking service. Use the booking-dev endpoint and booking-db connection. Read the reservations schema and summarize reservations by status. Do not change data. Include the connection name in your result.

These are example tasks you can reproduce with the demo's data. They give you something concrete to review: which service was used, what was read, and whether the answer addresses the correct application.

Explicit instructions help the agent choose tools, but they are not an access-control mechanism. Pair them with the workspace configuration and endpoint permissions described above.

This follows a useful theme in Alex Cloudstar's HackerNoon account of an AI coding workflow: write the constraints before asking the agent to work. Here, those constraints include the service access available to each task.

Parallel work needs both endpoints available. At other times, you may want to concentrate on the store and temporarily stop new requests to the booking services.

Turn Access off on booking-dev. GateRook preserves the endpoint's tool modes, tokens, and settings, while blocking new service operations through that endpoint. shop-dev stays enabled.

Turn it back on when you need that project again. There is no need to recreate the connections or replace the endpoint URL.

The switch applies to every client using that endpoint. If another conversation is actively investigating the booking service, pausing booking-dev also blocks its new service requests. Treat this as a shared access control, not a private switch for the chat you happen to be viewing.

Also, do not assume switching off cancels an operation already in progress. The useful guarantee for this workflow is control over subsequent requests.

Sometimes the database is still useful but the cache is not. Perhaps you are checking whether an answer can be derived entirely from persisted records.

Turn shop-cache off and leave shop-db on. The endpoint stays enabled, and the database remains available under its existing rules.

New service operations through that endpoint, across all its connections

New operations on that connection across every endpoint that uses it

Whether a particular tool is allowed, requires approval, or is off for that endpoint

In this demo, each connection belongs to one project endpoint. If you later share a connection between endpoints, its connection switch affects all of them. Use endpoint-specific tool modes when the restriction should apply to only one access path.

An off connection may still be discoverable, allowing the AI to ask you to enable it. Off means operations are blocked; it does not necessarily mean the client removes every reference to the service.

Before starting a task, check the workspace, endpoint, and enabled services. When reviewing a result, check which connection supplied the data. When putting a project aside, decide whether its endpoint should remain available to other ongoing work.

Keep the limits of this arrangement clear. Switching access does not erase information already in a conversation. GateRook governs requests routed through it; an agent's separate shell tools or direct credentials are outside that path. And although service credentials stay in GateRook, tool results can still enter the AI application's context and reach its model provider.

The practical benefit is a setup you can inspect and change quickly: two project contexts in one AI environment, two named service-access paths, and controls for pausing either a whole project or one connection. When both projects are active, leave both available. When the task narrows, narrow the access with it.

#9707. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

#9706. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9705. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

#9704. Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

1. Get very excited about it 2. See if we could either: A. Stick it in our shorts B. See if it could be made a good weapon C. Amuse ourselves with it to the point of unconsciousness with it, or D. Enrich ourselves with it.

Unfortunately, ancient humans, when they picked up a rock, thought first about who they could bash over the head with it, not build a hospital.

I exaggerate a bit to make a point. We’ve come a little way since then, but that old hard-wiring is hard to erase. I imagine that, AI being made in our own image, will follow a similar course if not VERY strictly overseen.

#9703. U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering

The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

#9702. When AI Localization Translates a Promise You Cannot Keep

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Hero illustration. Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

The translated page reads beautifully. The call to action works. The search annotations pass a technical check.

The page also promises a product feature that is not available in the reader's market.

Translation quality did not prevent the failure because the failure was not linguistic. A commercial claim crossed a regional boundary without being checked against regional facts.

I would treat AI localization as a release process for a local promise, not merely a process for producing text in another language. Fluency, product accuracy, technical delivery, and search configuration need separate checks.

A language can serve several markets. A market can require several languages. Neither alone determines product eligibility, currency, commercial terms, or the correct sales destination.

Start by identifying the intended audience precisely enough for the decision. A Spanish-language educational article may serve readers across regions, while a product offer may require market-specific availability and terms.

Do not create unnecessary regional copies merely because a localization tool can generate them. Each additional version creates a maintenance obligation and another place where a promise can drift.

Conversely, do not force materially different offers into one universal translated page. If the underlying product or commercial facts differ, the content architecture needs to preserve that difference rather than hide it in a vague footnote.

The proposed design is a matrix of language, market, product scope, and intended action. It is not a claim that every company needs a separate URL for every combination. The right structure depends on the actual differences that readers need to understand.

A shared claim might explain a general workflow or product concept. A local fact might state an available payment method, support arrangement, product edition, price, tax treatment, or delivery condition.

Keep local facts in a reviewed source of record rather than asking the translation model to infer them. A model can preserve approved values or flag missing ones; it should not choose a plausible regional offer because the source page lacks detail.

For each consequential fact, record its owner, effective date, scope, and review condition. Product marketing may own feature descriptions, while finance or the relevant commercial team owns approved pricing. Legal terms require the appropriate review rather than a linguistic approximation.

Do not confuse a disclaimer with a correction. A large promise at the top of a page remains misleading if a small note below quietly withdraws it for most readers.

The local version should state the applicable promise clearly where the reader makes the decision. If the correct fact is unknown, hold the affected claim or action until it can be verified.

Imagine a software company translating a page from English into German. The source says the product includes a particular payment capability. The capability is available only in selected markets and editions.

The translator preserves the sentence accurately. The local page is therefore faithful to the source and still wrong for part of its intended audience.

A better workflow attaches eligibility conditions to the claim before translation. The German page can then use the approved local statement or omit the unsupported promise. A language reviewer should not be expected to discover product entitlement rules from prose alone.

Now add a displayed price. Replacing a dollar sign with a euro sign is not currency conversion, local pricing approval, or tax treatment. Even a correctly formatted number can communicate the wrong commercial offer.

This is a constructed example, not a report about a particular product. It shows why translation accuracy and local business accuracy need independent sign-off. Neither check can safely stand in for the other.

A local promise needs three independent checks. Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

The JavaScript Internationalization API's number-formatting documentation illustrates locale-sensitive currency and numeric presentation. Formatting can change separators, symbols, and displayed precision.

It does not decide the business value being formatted. A formatting function does not set a local price, apply an exchange-rate policy, or determine which taxes belong in a quoted offer.

Keep value calculation, commercial approval, and presentation separate. Test dates, percentages, units, ranges, and decimal precision as well as currency. A decimal or date ambiguity can alter an implementation instruction even when the surrounding translation is clear.

Do not rely only on screenshots. Validate the underlying structured values and the resulting visible text. A page can look plausible while its downloadable document, form confirmation, or checkout uses a different amount.

For technical content, preserve units explicitly. A translated performance claim needs the original measurement basis and conditions, not merely a localized numeral. If the source lacks that context, localization should reveal the gap rather than make the claim sound more authoritative.

Google's guidance on localized page versions explains annotations for language and regional alternatives. Language-only tags can be valid; a country code is not mandatory for every page.

The implementation should reflect actual alternatives and follow documented requirements, including reciprocal relationships where applicable. A technically correct annotation does not verify the offer or guarantee that a particular URL will appear for every user.

Google's multi-regional and multilingual guidance also recommends distinct URLs for language versions and warns about approaches that can make variations hard to discover.

This is why an SEO checklist and a product-accuracy checklist must remain separate. Correct search signals can help describe the site's structure. They cannot repair an unavailable feature, an incorrect price, or an unsupported regional claim.

Do not manufacture regional pages with only a translated heading and unchanged main content. The visible content should be useful for the audience the page claims to serve, not merely a technical entry in an alternate-language set.

W3C's guidance on declaring language in HTML describes using the language attribute for the page and marking passages in another language where appropriate.

That supports processing and accessibility. It is not identical to Google's use of visible content to determine page language, nor is it a replacement for localized-version annotations.

Keep these mechanisms distinct in review. The document language, visible language, alternative-page relationships, and commercial market can each be correct or incorrect independently.

Test navigation, form labels, validation messages, and confirmation screens, not only the article body. A reader should not encounter a translated promise followed by an unexplained language switch at the action point.

Also provide a usable way to choose another language or market where appropriate. A visitor's location does not necessarily establish their language preference or purchasing entity. Avoid trapping people in an inferred version that they cannot change.

A useful instruction identifies the audience, terminology, approved claims, immutable values, and unresolved local facts. Ask the system to flag conflicts rather than resolve them creatively.

For example, it can preserve an approved product name, translate an explanatory paragraph, and return a review note that the payment-method statement lacks a verified regional version. That is more useful than a fluent guess.

Separate language suggestions from factual edits. A reviewer should be able to see whether the model changed style, altered a number, removed a qualification, or introduced a new capability claim.

Use a glossary, but do not treat it as complete proof of quality. The same term can require different phrasing in a user interface, technical article, and legal document. Context and qualified human review still matter.

Back-translation can reveal some differences, but it is not a complete validation method. A model can translate an incorrect promise consistently in both directions. The factual source must be checked independently of linguistic consistency.

A locale release card can make the review concrete:

This is a proposed review artifact, not a requirement to expand a simple educational page into a large approval system. Apply greater scrutiny where an incorrect local promise could cause a consequential decision, and keep the process lighter where the content makes no regional commercial claim.

Choose representative page types and high-risk claims. Verify the approved local facts, visible copy, metadata, language declarations, alternative links, forms, downloadable assets, and final action destination.

Include negative cases. What happens when a capability is unavailable in the selected market? Does the page say so clearly, or does it continue to offer a misleading action? What happens when the local price has not been approved?

Test mobile layouts and text expansion. A qualification that is present but clipped, hidden, or separated from the promise may fail the reader even though a text comparison says it exists.

Record the review scope. One reviewed page does not validate an entire language site. A translation vendor's approval of wording does not establish that the checkout or campaign destination matches the offer.

The release decision should state which locales and page versions were verified, which remain held, and who owns unresolved factual questions. A batch status of translated is not a sufficient readiness state.

When a shared source changes, identify the local versions and derivative campaigns that depend on the changed claim. Do not blindly overwrite every locale with a new translation if the local product facts differ.

Classify the change. A corrected typo, a new feature entitlement, and a revised price require different review paths. Some updates can propagate mechanically; others require a local decision before release.

Keep an effective-date record so the team can explain which version a reader encountered. If an earlier page was materially incorrect, review the appropriate correction and customer communication process rather than simply replacing the file and forgetting it.

Useful measures include unresolved local facts, stale versions awaiting review, broken alternative relationships, and mismatches between the page and its action destination. These are process indicators, not promises of ranking or revenue improvement.

AI makes producing another language version easier. The durable advantage is keeping each version connected to a promise the business can actually fulfill. Fluent translation opens the conversation. Accurate local facts are what allow the company to stand behind it.

Retargeting Has a State-Synchronization Problem

Attributed Revenue Cannot Tell You What Your Ads Caused

#9701. DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

Adapted from the original RadixArk article.

Advancements in model post-training are interesting because they can improve how efficiently models handle specialized tasks and complex instructions. For businesses building AI-powered applications, selecting the right model is also an important cost consideration. A larger model is not always necessary for every task, and using appropriately sized models can help balance performance, latency, and API expenses. I've been exploring how model selection and resource optimization influence the overall cost of AI agent systems. This guide shares practical approaches to optimizing AI agent costs: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-agent-cost-optimization

#9700. Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site

U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.
