#9689. I Built a React Tool to Trace Where a 464 ms Click Spent Its Time

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I clicked Log in on a demo page. Chrome measured 464 ms from the click to the next paint. That was the page’s Interaction to Next Paint (INP) at the time. Okay, so the click was slow. I still needed to figure out where the time went.

So I built react-inp-blame. It lines up the browser’s interaction timings with what React committed. The login report showed 405 ms of processing. It leaned toward the click handler because only two components re-rendered.

I started it on September 12, 2026. 0.1.0 was on npm five days later and 1.0.0 came out on October 10. No runtime dependencies, MIT license. Everything I show below runs on the live demo, so you can go click the same buttons.

On most pages, INP is the latency of the longest interaction. On busier pages it drops one high outlier for every 50 interactions. Chrome’s tools and web-vitals break the interaction down into input delay, processing and presentation.

From the press until the first event handler starts

Your handler code, and in React, the render it triggers

From the end of the handlers until the next paint

Which is useful, up to a point. In a React app "processing" is your onClick plus React's render plus whatever effects ran along the way, all lumped together, and the thing you clicked is a button nested a few components deep. When you actually sit down to fix it you want something smaller and more annoying. Which component? Which handler? How many renders? Was it even React?

React DevTools can answer some of it, if you had the profiler recording at the moment the slow click happened. Usually you didn't.

The demo is a fake photo app called Framely with a sign-in page that has a few realistic mistakes baked in. Nothing leaves the page, the sign-in is simulated.

After the sign-in, a small dark badge in the bottom left corner shows the page's INP so far. It's green at 200 ms or under, amber up to 500 and red above that.

Click the badge and you get a panel of the recent slow interactions. Click a row and it opens up with the full explanation. My run for this article had 24 interactions in it, 15 key presses in the email field, 8 in the password field, and the one click.

The typing shows a different problem. Each key press in the email field re-rendered 1,004 components, 1,000 of them PostTile cards inside a FeedPreview that sits next to the form and has nothing to do with the email. The slowest key press took 232 ms and the typical one 160. The password field went the other way. Hardly anything rendered there, the time was in its own onChange handler, and the slowest press was 168 ms.

Then there's the second half of the login story, and honestly it's the part I care about most. React rendered again 274 ms after the screen had already updated, 256 components this time and most of them PhotoTile. INP doesn't count that render at all, cause it happened after the paint the click was waiting on. Whether it really belongs to the click is a harder question, I'll get to that.

Funny thing is the browser and React already know all of this between them. They just don't share.

Event Timing gives me the interaction ID and its timing. The Long Animation Frames API records the scripts in a long frame and their forced style and layout time. For the React side I listen to the same developer tools hook that React DevTools uses. After a commit, the library walks the fiber tree and counts what rendered.

Matching them up is where it got hard. The library keeps its last eight inputs and uses event timestamps to associate commits with an interaction. A render that lands after the next paint is listed as a follow-up with its own timing. The report leaves its trigger open when the timing is the only evidence.

None of this is a stable React API, so the library checks what it reads and fails closed. If react-dom is outside 17 to 19, or the fiber tree looks different from what it expects, it switches that part off, warns once, and keeps reporting, just without component names.

The demo also has an anti-pattern lab. It's eight slow interactions, each one built around one specific mistake, and a fast one as the control. I ran every scenario once on the live site, production build, and wrote down what the library said.

Every section rebuilt from scratch during render. 251 components inside SlowRender, mostly Section

Layout effects write a style, then read a size. 881 ms of forced style and layout, PriceTicker ×400

One class change restyles 30,000 cells. 773 ms updating the screen, browser work, no script

3,000 rows re-render on each key. 1,441 components inside BigList, mostly Row

Context value is a new object every render. 801 components, 800 LineItem inside OrderSummary

Input state lives above a heavy sidebar. 602 components, 600 NavItem inside Sidebar

The click handler burns 120 ms, nothing renders. The onClick handler, 120 ms

An effect sets more state after the click commits. A 401-component render 100 ms after the paint

Nothing, it's the control. No report, nothing stood out

Same nine interactions in the chart below, split by phase. Six are mostly "working", and that's the phase where a component or handler name is actually useful. Restyle storm is nearly all "updating the screen", where a React name won't help you at all.

I kept layout thrash in the lab cause it fooled me first. It looks exactly like a React problem. 400 rows, each one sets a style in a layout effect and then reads its own size back, and the browser has to redo layout 400 times inside a single commit. In the Performance panel it's one big purple and yellow block and you'd blame React for it.

Without the long-frame timing, the report would put roughly 1.1 seconds under processing. With it, I can see how much the browser spent recalculating styles and layout. Here’s what the report said.

Restyle storm goes one step further, there's basically no script in it. React renders a single component. Then one class change makes the browser restyle 30,000 cells, and that alone is 773 ms of "updating the screen" after the handler is long done (735 ms of it is the browser's own main thread work). No component name helps here. You fix it with fewer cells or CSS containment and React doesn't come into it.

Handler hog is the boring one and I like it for that. The onClick burns 120 ms, React renders nothing, and the report says so in one line. Nobody goes digging through the component tree for a render that never happened.

Cascading effect has an INP of 16 ms. Any dashboard would call that a perfect click.

Here's what's really going on. The click commits a tiny change, an effect picks it up and sets more state, and React renders again, 401 components this time, about 100 ms after the screen already updated. INP stops at the next paint, so it stops right before the expensive bit and never sees it.

I got the wording of this note wrong at first. Up to 0.25 it said people still wait for that render, which sounds right until you run it on a real app. On hyperdx, one of the two apps it was graded on, the render after a click was more than once a live tail's timer or a route change, nothing to do with the click. So from 0.26.0 the note only says INP doesn't count it and what started it can't be told. You still get the count and the time, it just doesn't pin it on a click it may not belong to.

One package, and on most apps one line in the build config. Vite:

Next.js 14.2 or later wraps the config instead:

Next.js 15.3 to 16.2 want one more export in instrumentation-client.ts. The wrapper keeps printing that line at you until the file has it, which is annoying on purpose. React Router in framework mode, Remix, TanStack Start and Astro all write their own HTML, so each gets its own short setup in the docs.

Both plugins only run in development unless you say otherwise. With the defaults a production build gets nothing from them (on Next.js 15.3 to 16.2 the extra export stays in, as an empty function).

CI covers react-dom 17.0.2 up to 19.3.0 plus React canary, Next.js 14.2.35 up to 16.3.5 plus canary, and Vite 6.4, 7.3 and 8.3. It also installs the packed tarball into fresh apps from create-vite, create-react-router, TanStack Start's CLI and create astro, then checks that a slow click there still gets blamed on the right component. That last part caught more bugs than the unit tests did.

Most teams already ship INP somewhere and I didn't want to replace that. The web-vitals attribution build keeps doing the measuring and this adds the React part on top. The lightest setup doesn't even need the runtime on the page, only the build step that keeps component names around:

You need web-vitals 5.1 or later for that. If you want the full report, the docs have the attributeINP path, sent on to Sentry or GA4.

There's also react-inp-blame/otel, still experimental. It adds the blame to the INP event an OpenTelemetry web vitals pipeline already sends, as react_inp_blame.* attributes, so you can group and filter on it in Honeycomb, Elastic, Embrace or Grafana Faro. It doesn't import anything from OpenTelemetry or a vendor SDK. Experimental just means the attribute names could still change in a minor release, cause OpenTelemetry's browser conventions have no field yet for an interaction's target or a component.

A tool for slow clicks that makes clicks slower would be a bad joke. Every report carries overheadMs, the library's own time for that interaction, so I couldn't really hide from it even if I wanted to.

The repo's numbers are 30 fresh page loads per scenario on two of the heaviest demo scenarios, a click that re-renders 801 components and a key press that re-renders 1,441:

In my own sign-in run for this article the 24 reports cost 0.1 to 3.2 ms each. The one outlier was the first key press on the page at 12 ms. Lab scenarios came in at 0.5 to 5.6 ms, one interaction each.

Size is the other cost if you turn it on in production:

react-inp-blame/auto, everything that loads with the page

The badge and panel, loaded only when shown

react-inp-blame/web-vitals, on top of /auto

35.8 KB gzip is real weight. That's why production is opt-in with a sampleRate, and why the web-vitals path with no runtime exists at all.

The demo's header says "It can be wrong". I put that there and I meant it.

Treat a component name as a lead. In a production React build, the library uses component counts because it lacks render durations. The login report hedged between the handler and the render for that reason. Forced layout attribution also depends on the browser exposing Long Animation Frames.

Before 1.0 I set a bar for myself, at least 38 right and at most 6 wrong out of 62 verdicts on apps it had never seen. 0.25.0 got graded on two real open-source apps, hyperdx and kaneo. It got 8 right, 35 wrong and 19 misleading. So no, the bar isn't met, and the 1.0.0 changelog says that in plain words. What 1.0 promises is the API and the report shape, the fields keep their meaning through 1.x. Accuracy isn't part of that promise yet.

The next round is five everyday open-source React apps, Actual, myfin, Kresus, Manage My Damn Life and Reactive Resume. The protocol freezes the test cases before anyone looks at what the library says about them. Their integrations are still being built, so no results yet. If it blames the wrong thing on your app there's an issue form just for that, and honestly those reports help more than anything else.

Quickest way is the demo at reactinpblame.com. Everything on it is slow on purpose. Click around, read what the badge blames, then open the Performance panel in DevTools and check it, the library draws its own track there next to React's.

Add the Vite plugin or the Next.js wrapper from above, restart the dev server and click the slowest thing you know about. Code, docs and known limits are on GitHub, and the package is on npm.

#9688. How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on.

Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it.

The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments.

In the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent. The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across.

AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes.

Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms, teams managed by an orchestrator, and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work. Figure 1 shows a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations.

Figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced.

We’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench, researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed.

Figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation.

There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately.

Demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party, and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough.

With the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation.

We work through eight steps: define the claim, find a task, run it unchanged, adapt it, check the evaluation, read the traces, report the score, and compare models. We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A. Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example.

Figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel shows what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results.

Claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A). For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio (the intensity of one peak relative to another, which can indicate defects in the material; we also call it the defect ratio), and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Starting task and baseline. We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. Harbor is an open source evaluation harness, and Terminal-Bench is an open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a terminal. We first ran the task's reference solution, which passed, and then ran the original task three times with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI. Harbor ran inside an HF Job, each rollout used its own HF Sandbox, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. Only the agent harness needed no new work. Every other component needed checking or new work, which we list part by part at the end of Appendix A.

Adaptation. We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. The new instructions state the units and parameter definitions that the original left implicit. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

Checks. Before executing more model runs, we tested the evaluation itself. We ran the reference solution, an agent that does nothing, and a shortcut that skips the required work. The reference solution should pass every task, and the other two should fail. Our shortcut read the height of each peak straight from the data and guessed the widths. It returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself.

Shortcut. We also tested a shortcut to check how robust the evaluation is against cheating. Our shortcut is a short script that skips the actual fitting. It reads the tallest point of each peak straight from the data, guesses the peak widths, and divides the D height by the G height. Even so, it returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks, so a grader that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks. We added checks on each fitted peak, and the final verifier rejects it.

Figure 4. What we learned by measuring different aspects while building the evaluation. (A) Testing the grader with a shortcut showed that a ratio-only check could be fooled. (B) Reading gpt-oss-120b’s traces showed that most of its failures came from stopping early. (C) Running other models showed that the tasks can be solved. Appendix A has the detailed results in Figure 7 (how gpt-oss-120b’s attempts ended), Figure 8 (all six models) and Figure 9 (when each model said it was done).

Baseline. On the original task, gpt-oss-120b passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

Traces and score. On the eight adapted tasks, we ran three rollouts per task. The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file. Several of these began with a script failing because NumPy or SciPy was missing, which the task expects the agent to install. Most failures therefore came from stopping early or from a missing package, and only two of the 13 failed the fit check (Figure 7 in Appendix A). Our pass@3 was 7/8: seven tasks succeeded at least once. Our pass^3 was 1/8: one task succeeded every time. Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more. The mean pass rate was 0.46, with a standard error of about 0.11 when rollouts are clustered by task. A repeat run passed 10 of 24. With eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to new spectra.

Model comparison. We then compared six models on the same eight tasks (Figure 4). Several providers can serve the same open-weight model with different quantization and context limits, so we pinned one provider per model. With DeepInfra pinned as the provider, gpt-oss-120b passed 13 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the earlier run, which used the default provider. Only gpt-oss-120b declared completion in its first response, in 22 of 24 rollouts. None of the other five models did so in any rollout (Figure 9 in Appendix A). The comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio without fitting a spectrum. A verifier that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks on all eight tasks. We found it by trying to break the grader with a solution we knew was incomplete, then added checks on the fitted spectrum (Appendix A, Step 5).

The shortcut got the right answer for the wrong reason, like a student who copies the final number without the working. The lesson for us was to test what the output demonstrates. A faster valid method should pass; a method that skips a required skill should not. Domain experts can help set tolerances so the verifier accepts alternative correct fits without accepting work that misses the point of the task.

Such errors are common, and they move scores considerably. A review of agentic benchmarks found that flaws in task setup or reward design can shift measured performance by up to 100% in relative terms.

Public review can expose errors in instructions and tests that benchmark builders missed. Terminal-Bench 2.1 fixed 28 of its 89 tasks after user reports, including one whose tests expected Spark SQL while its instructions asked for PostgreSQL, and agent rankings stayed stable through the correction.

Access to the evidence also determines how much work an outside audit takes. CritPt keeps its reference solutions private, so the physicists who audited it had to solve the problems themselves before finding errors in 21 of the 56 challenges they reviewed. The authors then released a corrected version. OpenAI's audit of SWE-bench Verified found material issues in 59.4% of the 138 problems it examined, working from tasks and tests that anyone can read. For a builder, outside scrutiny is part of validation: publish what reviewers need to challenge a task, give them a way to report problems, and record what changed.

Similar flaws emerged in SWE-bench Pro. In July 2026 OpenAI estimated that about 30% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks were broken and withdrew its recommendation to adopt it. Benchmark validation needs to continue after release.

A consistent score can still measure the wrong thing. Measuring what Matters, a review of 445 LLM benchmarks by 29 expert reviewers, found recurring patterns in tasks and metrics that undermine construct validity: whether the tasks and metrics support claims about the intended capability.

For example, fitting synthetic spectra does not establish that an agent can review lab reports. That may also require recognizing a poor measurement or asking for help. If every task supplies a usable spectrum, the test cannot show whether the agent knows when a fit would be inappropriate.

Harder Than the Task extends this concern to organizational work, where authority, distributed knowledge, and dependencies can decide success. Its authors find that fewer than one quarter of prominent benchmarks claim to cover any such dimension. An agent may need calibration data from another team or permission to replace a measurement, and supplying everything at the outset removes those difficulties. If they matter to the claim, they belong in the evaluation. If they do not, it is enough to say that they remain untested.

Each error is worth a short record: the failed assumption, how it was found, and what changed. The record should also name the affected versions and say whether earlier scores remain comparable.

The SWE-bench Verified audit described above also found contamination: every frontier model tested could reproduce the reference patch or verbatim problem details for some tasks. SWE-bench's public repositories and wide use exposed tasks to training. The openness that enabled scrutiny of bad tests also made items easier to encounter before evaluation.

However, if contamination is carefully controlled for during training, hiding the test set by itself does not prevent saturation. A study of 60 language model benchmarks found similar saturation in public and private ones, and concluded that hiding test data does not prevent saturation once a benchmark is widely adopted, meaning a good benchmark falls out of use due to saturation without developers being able to learn from and build on it. What did correspond to lower saturation was expert curation and a larger test set.

This leaves a practical release question: what can we expose for review while protecting active test items?

Balancing contamination risks against saturation requires a strategic approach to what content is made public. Rather than treating openness as an all-or-nothing decision, benchmark creators can decide what to release part by part, protecting active test tasks from data leakage while still sharing the underlying infrastructure, grading methods, and reference examples that allow external researchers to audit and build upon the evaluation.

Existing benchmarks show a range of openness. ARC-AGI-2 publishes a training set and a 120-task evaluation set, and holds back semi-private and private sets of 120 tasks each. AILuminate keeps its official prompts confidential, publishes its methods and taxonomy, and keeps the underlying evidence for controlled review by authorized auditors and trusted researchers. Terminal-Bench publishes its tasks and marks their files with a canary string asking that they stay out of training corpora. No public reviewer can check a protected item, so whatever stays closed needs a review route of its own.

Table 1 outlines the core considerations of open sourcing an evaluation: what can be open, where it lives on the Hugging Face Hub, and what may stay protected. It has one row for each component in Figure 2, so you can go straight to the part you are about to release.

Table 1. What to open, how to share it on the Hugging Face Hub, and what can stay protected, for each evaluation component.

Our own example follows this approach. We released raman-lab as a dataset on the Hub. It includes eight synthetic graphene spectra in Harbor task format, each with its environment, reference fit, verifier, and tolerances. The raw rollouts behind our results are shared as a separate dataset including Harbor trial folders with trajectories and verifier output for all six models. The spectrum generator, analysis code, and results are in a companion GitHub repository, so both the agent harness and the evaluation harness can be inspected and rerun.

In a more sensitive domain, a clinical evaluation could open its environment definition, harness, tool interfaces, and grading framework, with synthetic cases for development use. Patient records and reference answers would stay under controlled access while authorized reviewers inspect disputed judgments. Each restriction should come with a condition for revisiting it.

We recommend a short checklist, drawn in part from the more comprehensive Agentic Benchmark Checklist. Before releasing or retiring an evaluation, check that another builder can:

These release decisions also determine what remains useful when the benchmark no longer separates the systems it was built to compare.

Benchmarks have a lifecycle. They are built, adopted, optimized against, and in time stop separating the systems they were made to compare. The saturation study from section 3 rated 29 of its 60 language model benchmarks as highly saturated, with rates rising with age. Saturation is not a failure in itself, since it can mean the capability has arrived.

What a benchmark leaves behind depends on how open it was. Publishing only scores leaves future builders little they can run or adapt. When the tasks, environments, verifiers, and traces are open, each keeps working after the leaderboard stops. A solved task becomes a regression check for a new harness. Its environment and verifier can seed a harder successor. Open benchmarks also get repaired and reissued: MMLU's questions became MMLU-Redux, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 became 2.1 through community contributions. Our own walkthrough is an afterlife of this kind: raman-lab began as one task in a benchmark built for general terminal work.

That is the promise of building evaluations openly. The work that goes into an evaluation can outlive the benchmark itself, giving others a foundation to ask new questions, test new capabilities, and improve on what came before. The more we share what we build and learn, the less each new evaluation has to start from scratch.

If you’re curious what this looks like in practice, then follow our practical example.

Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. Raman spectroscopy shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the frequency of the scattered light; the resulting peaks reveal properties of the material. For graphene, an atom-thick sheet of carbon, the G and 2D peaks near 1580 and 2700 cm⁻¹ identify the number of layers. A third peak, D, appears when the lattice is disordered, and its intensity relative to G can indicate defects. Figure 5 shows the setup.

Figure 5. Our intended setup. A laser lights a graphene sample, and a spectrometer records how the scattered light has shifted. The agent receives that spectrum as a file, fits a curve to each peak, and saves the fitted values. The verifier checks the saved values against reference fits. The curve shown is a sketch, not measured data.

We start by building on a task from an open benchmark. Terminal-Bench 2 already includes raman-fitting: fit a Lorentzian curve, a mathematical peak shape, to each of those two peaks and save eight parameters to /app/results.json. That gives us a runnable starting point for a narrower lab evaluation. We run these on the open source evaluation harness, Harbor. Table 2 lists what the task provides and what to check before reusing each part.

Table 2. What to check before reusing each component.

A good place to start is a claim: a plain statement of what the agent can do, which the evaluation is meant to support. "The agent can fit a Raman spectrum" is a claim, and so is "the agent can process a lab report." From there, you can break the claim into smaller skills that can be checked one at a time, such as reading the file, locating the peaks, and writing the output.

For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio, and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Domain experts can help here. We suggest asking them to choose realistic noise levels, tolerances, and available software, then score examples independently and investigate disagreements. From there, you can break the claim into parts you can check and map each part to what each task tests.

For your own domain, the Hugging Face Hub is a good place to look, under its Benchmark and Environment dataset types. When you find a candidate, it is worth inspecting its instructions, environment, reference solution, and tests. Even a task that models already solve can provide useful infrastructure. From raman-fitting we inherit a working task format. It has only one spectrum, though, and a lab's measurements vary, so we expand on this task further as described in Step 4.

Before running any model, it helps to run the reference solution (also called oracle). If it fails, the fault lies in the task, environment, or verifier, and needs to be fixed before you read anything into model failures. After that, you can run the model several times without changing the setup.

We ran Harbor inside an HF Job, which supplied compute for the runner. Each rollout used its own HF Sandbox for commands and files, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. With Harbor's hf-sandbox extra installed and HF_TOKEN set, these commands test the oracle, then run three rollouts with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI.

In these commands, -t names the task, -a the agent, -e the environment, -m the model, and -k the number of rollouts per task.

The model passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

The D-to-G intensity ratio can indicate defects, but its interpretation depends on the laser excitation energy and the disorder regime. An evaluation asking for a "defect ratio" must say which peaks, whether intensity means height or integrated area, and how the result is checked.

The original instruction.md shows why such definitions matter: it asks for x0, gamma, amplitude, and offset without defining them or their units. The reference solution treats them as peak center, half-width at half-maximum, height above background, and background level, and converts the x-axis from nanometres to Raman shift. We put choices like these into the adapted instructions, so that the verifier's requirements are visible. Figure 6 shows the two files side by side.

Figure 6. The instruction.md files for raman-fitting and raman-lab, side by side. The highlighted additions cover the new parts of the claim: the D peak, the defect ratio, and both in the saved results. The remaining part, handling varied measurements, lives in the data: all eight raman-lab tasks share this instruction, and only the spectrum, with its noise and defect level, changes.

The shared format can stay as it is while the data and checks change. This command creates a task scaffold:

Before executing more model runs, test the evaluation itself. Here datasets/my-evals contains the adapted tasks.

Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself. Section 3 explains what that means for verifier design.

It is helpful to read both successful and failed rollouts. Harbor records messages, tool calls, and observations in agent/trajectory.json using ATIF, a shared trace format. Grouping failures by cause makes the patterns easier to see: parsing the data, executing a tool, stopping too early, or grading the output.

The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file.

Figure 7. On 19 of 24 attempts, the agent called mark_task_complete in its first response. Eleven produced no results file, seven passed, and one failed the fit check. Of the five remaining attempts, four passed and one failed the fit check.

Several missing-file failures began with missing NumPy or SciPy. The published task expects the agent to install them; its reference solution starts with a pip install. A lab evaluation of fitting with supplied tools could install and pin them in advance. Dependencies also drift: Terminal-Bench 2.1 repaired nine tasks whose external dependencies had changed after release.

Preinstalling changes the evaluation condition, so keep the model, harness, tasks, and rollout count fixed when comparing the two setups.

Finally, we adapt the setup, repeat the checks in step 5, and rerun. Harbor's trace exporter can prepare records for sharing on the Hub. It is worth reviewing them for protected content first, and keeping both successes and failures so others can investigate the result.

The right metric depends on the decision you need to make:

Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more.

A mean is more useful with its uncertainty beside it. Rollouts of the same spectrum share its difficulty, so they are not independent, and the standard error should be clustered by task. Clustering gave a mean success rate of 0.46 with a standard error of about 0.11. A repeat run passed 10 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the first run. With only eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to new spectra.

Harbor writes a result.json per rollout, which it calls a trial. We group these by task, check that each task has three rollouts, and record errors or exclusions. Reporting tokens, elapsed time, and tool calls beside the score lets readers compare setups that reach similar results at different costs.

When a single model fails a task, that run alone cannot tell us what went wrong. It could be the model, the agent harness, or the evaluation itself. Running more models on the same tasks helps narrow the possibilities. When several models fail the same task, inspect the instructions, environment, and verifier for a shared cause. When one model repeatedly fails in a distinctive way, compare its traces with successful attempts.

Inference Providers serves many open-weight models through the same router, so each new model is one more value for -m. Several providers can serve the same model with different quantization and context limits, so it helps to pin one with a suffix such as :deepinfra and record it beside the score.

Figure 8 shows the raman-lab results for each model.

Figure 8. raman-lab results per model, with pass@3, pass^3, and the mean pass rate with its clustered standard error. Select a square to inspect that rollout.

The comparison makes one pattern in gpt-oss-120b clearer: it often declares completion before seeing command output. In this separate run with DeepInfra pinned as the provider, it called mark_task_complete in its first response in 22 of 24 rollouts, while none of the other five models did so (Figure 9). The Step 6 run used the router's default provider and recorded 19 of 24 such early completions. It passed 11 of 24 rollouts, compared with 13 of 24 in the DeepInfra run. Both counts use the same test: whether the model called mark_task_complete in its first response.

Figure 9. raman-lab rollout outcomes by when the agent declared completion. Left: the agent observed command output first. Right: it called mark_task_complete in its first response.

The comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Inference for all six models cost under $5 at the router's list prices. The median raman-lab rollout used about 6,000 tokens for gpt-oss-120b and about 90,000 for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash. The companion repository holds the traces, the per-rollout results, and the scripts to add another model.

Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. We could reuse them because Harbor and Terminal-Bench publish their code and tasks.

Task: We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. The new work was a narrower claim, skill coverage, and instructions for raman-lab.

Task data: The original spectrum served as a starting example. We built a generator for eight spectra with known parameters and reviewed them manually.

Environment: Harbor's environment support and HF Sandbox ran the tasks. We checked package requirements and diagnosed missing dependencies.

Agent harness and tools: Terminus-2 with shell access, with Inference Providers for model responses. This part needed no new work.

Rollout and trace: Harbor's rollout records and ATIF captured each run. We reviewed successes and failures and grouped them by cause.

Reference solution: We kept the convention of running solution/solve.sh and wrote a reference fit for each new task.

Evaluation harness: Harbor ran in an HF Job. We configured the run and grouped results by task.

Verifier: We reused the tests/test.sh entry point and its way of writing the score to a file. The new work was fit and ratio checks, plus tests for shortcuts and incorrect outputs.

Agent harness: The software around a model that turns its responses into actions, such as shell commands. Terminus-2 is the agent harness in this post.

Agentic evaluation: An evaluation that scores what an agent changed in an environment, not only the text it returned.

ATIF: Agent Trajectory Interchange Format, a shared format for recording an agent's messages, tool calls and observations.

Canary string: A unique marker in benchmark files that lets model trainers find and exclude them from training data.

Clustered standard error: A standard error that treats rollouts of the same task as related, which gives a wider and more honest margin than treating each rollout as independent.

Container image: A fixed package of operating system, files and software, so every rollout starts from the same environment.

Contamination: Test questions or solutions appearing in training data, so a score may reflect memory rather than skill.

Context limit: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can read in one request.

D, G and 2D peaks: Features in graphene's Raman spectrum. G and 2D indicate the number of layers, and D appears when the carbon lattice has defects.

Defect ratio: The intensity of the D peak divided by that of the G peak, used to indicate defects in graphene. Also called the D-to-G ratio.

Development set: Tasks used while building and debugging an evaluation, as opposed to a held-back test set used for final scores.

Environment: The software, files and resources an agent works in during a task.

Evaluation harness: The software that runs tasks, repeats rollouts, collects traces and aggregates scores. Harbor is the evaluation harness in this post.

Gated dataset: A Hugging Face dataset that can be downloaded only after the owner approves an access request.

Harbor: An open-source evaluation harness for agentic tasks.

HF Job: Compute on Hugging Face that runs a script. Here it runs Harbor.

HF Sandbox: An isolated Hugging Face environment where a single rollout runs its commands and stores its files.

Held-out test set: Test items kept private so that models cannot be trained or tuned on them.

Inference Providers: A Hugging Face service that routes model requests to third-party providers through one API, called the router.

Lorentzian: A mathematical curve commonly used to model the shape of a spectral peak.

No-op agent: An agent that does nothing. A sound evaluation gives it a score of zero.

Open-weight model: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.

Oracle: An agent that runs the reference solution, used to check that every task can be solved in the supplied environment.

pass@k: The share of tasks where at least one of k rollouts succeeds.

pass^k: The share of tasks where all k rollouts succeed.

Pinning: Fixing the exact versions of software, images or model providers so a run can be repeated.

Quantization: Storing model weights at lower numerical precision to run faster and cheaper, which can change outputs slightly.

Raman shift: The difference in frequency between the laser light and the light a sample scatters, measured in cm⁻¹.

Raman spectroscopy: A technique that shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the scattered light to identify properties of the material.

Reference solution: A known correct way to complete a task, stored with the task.

Rollout: One attempt by an agent at one task. Harbor calls it a trial.

Run record: A record of what ran behind a score: the exact task, environment, model configuration and code versions.

Saturation: The point where most models reach top scores on a benchmark, so it no longer separates them.

Synthetic data: Data generated from known parameters, so the correct answer is known in advance.

Terminal-Bench: An open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a computer terminal.

Terminus-2: The terminal agent harness used in this post. It connects the model to shell commands.

Token: The unit of text a model reads and writes, roughly a short word or part of a word.

Trace: The full record of a rollout: the model's messages, its tool calls and what each command returned. Also called a trajectory.

Verifier: The code that grades a rollout by checking the saved output or the environment's final state.

Explore daily Hugging Face Hub statistics

Agentic evaluations are important for understanding how reliably AI agents perform across different tasks and scenarios. I think AI agent observability is equally valuable because tracking an agent’s behavior, decisions, and performance helps identify issues and improve results over time. This is also relevant to practical business applications such as automated customer verification, as discussed here: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-kyc-automation-customer-verification

#9687. Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?

The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

#9685. When Everyone Looks Qualified, Who Actually Is?

Human-Centered Transformation Navigating the AI Era with Purpose.

Human-Centered Transformation Navigating the AI Era with Purpose.

Human-Centered Transformation Navigating the AI Era with Purpose.

We've spent decades building systems that recognize achievement. AI is forcing us to reconsider how we recognize capability.

Spend enough time around startups and you'll recognize the pattern.

An ambitious founder. A compelling pitch deck. A product roadmap promising to transform an industry.

Investors get interested. People start talking. Talented employees leave secure jobs to join something that feels like the next big thing.

And somewhere along the way, the ability to tell a convincing story starts getting confused with the ability to deliver one.

Strategy meetings fill with ambitious promises. Deadlines slip. The people doing the difficult work begin losing confidence.

Eventually, the distance between the pitch and the product becomes impossible to ignore.

By then, good people have left, teams have burned out, and trust has eroded.

There's a particular kind of bullshit that thrives in environments where confidence is mistaken for competence.

Persuasion, of course, is an essential part of entrepreneurship. Great founders attract talent, capital, and belief long before their vision becomes reality. Some of the world's most successful companies began with ideas that seemed almost impossible.

The trouble begins when the ability to sell the vision outpaces the ability to execute it, and nobody recognizes the difference until the consequences arrive.

AI is making that distinction even harder.

In April 2026, recruitment firm Robert Half reported something revealing about Australian hiring managers.

While 97% expected new employees to have some proficiency with AI and automation, 88% were struggling to find candidates with the right AI and automation skills. More than a third said AI-generated résumés were making applicants harder to evaluate.

There's an uncomfortable contradiction here.

Employers increasingly expect people to work with AI, while the same technology is making it harder to determine what those people can actually do.

A candidate can arrive with an impressive résumé, a sophisticated portfolio, a working prototype, and a beautifully articulated strategy.

Some will have exercised extraordinary judgment in creating that work. Others may understand very little of what they're presenting.

And from the finished product alone, distinguishing between them is becoming increasingly difficult.

We've encountered versions of this problem in education for decades.

Two students earn the same grade. One has developed deep understanding through experimentation, feedback, and revision. The other has learned how to satisfy the assessment.

The learning behind it may be very different.

Now imagine those students graduating, entering the workforce, and eventually founding or leading organizations.

A degree opens a door. A résumé earns an interview. A portfolio demonstrates experience.

But what happens when the signals we've traditionally trusted become less revealing about the capabilities people have actually developed?

Consider a startup founder evaluating a developer with an impressive portfolio.

Clean interfaces. Working demonstrations. A GitHub profile filled with activity.

The founder could ask which AI tools the candidate uses, how quickly they built the applications, or what frameworks they know.

But imagine asking them to show the part that almost failed.

The architectural decision they got wrong.

The solution AI confidently recommended that they eventually rejected.

What made them question the original approach? What evidence changed their mind? What would they do differently today?

That conversation might reveal more about their capabilities than the finished portfolio ever could.

The cost of mistaking appearance for ability remains extraordinarily high.

There's a phrase from Web3 that feels especially relevant here. Proof of Work.

In blockchain, it refers to a mechanism for validating computational work and helping secure a network. I'm borrowing the phrase as a metaphor for something more human.

What if we became better at recognizing the thinking behind what people produce?

Consider the founder who abandoned a promising pitch after discovering that customers didn't actually need the product.

Or the designer who rejected their most visually impressive prototype because user testing exposed a fundamental flaw.

Or the graduate who challenged an AI-generated analysis, discovered that its assumptions were wrong, and rebuilt the argument from the evidence.

There's something revealing about the work people decide against doing.

The ideas they abandon. The shortcuts they refuse. The assumptions they reconsider.

Those decisions can reveal judgment, adaptability, and intellectual honesty.

This is where portfolios, meaningful data, and visible learning become valuable.

Imagine students graduating with evidence of projects, demonstrated skills, feedback, and how their thinking developed over time.

Founders presenting validated experiments and customer evidence alongside projections.

Employees being recognized for the problems they've solved, the independence they've developed, and the contributions they've made.

These records could tell richer stories about human capability.

Of course, AI can also manufacture convincing portfolios, reflections, and accounts of someone's process. Credible evidence still requires verification, authentic demonstrations, and the ability to apply what we've learned.

There may be a useful role here for portable digital credentials, including Web3 approaches that help establish where evidence originated and who verified it.

But the meaning of that evidence will always require judgment.

Every system of recognition shapes behavior.

Schools reward grades. Companies reward performance. Startups reward growth, momentum, and the ability to attract belief.

The questions someone asked. The assumptions they challenged. The mistakes they recognized. The ideas they had the judgment to abandon.

And imagine what might change if we became better at recognizing those moments.

A school that helps students see how their thinking has developed.

A founder who values the candidate who can explain a failed project as thoughtfully as a successful one.

An organization that recognizes the employee who quietly prevents a costly mistake.

An investor who looks beyond the pitch to understand the evidence and judgment behind it.

These are choices about what we value, what we measure, and what we encourage people to become.

They also connect to the central idea behind Designing for AGENCY: as intelligent machines become more capable, human judgment, independence, and responsibility become increasingly important.

Perhaps those are the qualities our systems should become better at recognizing.

Because when everyone looks qualified, the most interesting question may be:

Can you show me the thinking behind what you've built?

Human-Centered Transformation Navigating the AI Era with Purpose.

#9684. Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites

At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”

Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”

How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.

Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”

Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?

Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

I look forward to ’29, with a Democratic administration, and QUALIFIED Cabinet members, so I can, for example, report all the false medical advice ads on youtube. (sorry, there is, in fact, diabetes in Israel, etc, etc.)

CSP is still a bit flawed, but is probably the best defense we have against XSS (cross-site script injections). However, having CSP rules in place, would not have prevented this at all since this was a supply chain attack on a trusted provider. Even if they hosted the 3rd party scripts themselves, the downloaded script would have contained the malware. Once that’s running, game is over…. they’d just make simple requests to the malicious domain with the stolen information. The end-user would need to have something in place that prevented the outgoing traffic. Making this situation worse, is that many sites (due to incompetence) will put in CORS rules that effectively wildcard allowed origins. (a different attack, but one where you’d be able to make cross-site requests from a scam site with the user’s credentials) Unfortunately, AI supplies a lot of people with code that has these vulnerabilities already baked in… garbage in, garbage out…

My understanding is that this attack directed the JavaScript to download malware from several domains that were definitely not Optimizely domains, and very much would be caught by a competently implemented CSP.

CSP headers would have stopped that attack, but only if using Optimizely didn’t already require setting ‘strict-dynamic’, which requires nonces/hashes instead (those aren’t really foolproof… once they are able to inject a script they can steal those too) But let’s say the CSP headers stopped the attack, the attackers could still fallback to the initial injected code. The attacker would only lose the ability to dynamically update things. (it’d force them to update from the already compromised supplier…)

The problem is these sites uses those stupid content delivery networks and if you block them then you do not get the body of the site. As a security person this leads to a problem when trying to provide access for people in your organization. How can I provide you access to a site where i know these cdns are in place but you have to have it in order to do your job?

The line that stuck with me was Scott Helme’s point that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy — a site can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code being at fault. That is exactly why I have become sceptical of keeping my most sensitive secrets inside the browser at all, even in a well-regarded password manager. If a trusted script can be swapped for a malicious one, the safest place for a seed phrase or a master password is somewhere no web page, extension or third-party script can reach. That thinking is why, as the developer of GhostCore, I built it as a fully offline iOS vault for seed phrases, passwords, cards and offline 2FA, with no cloud sync and no network access for the vault itself. CSPs and script blockers help a lot, as this article shows, but for the credentials that would be catastrophic to lose, removing them from the browser entirely feels like the more durable fix.

And it will be specifically targeted when it becomes used by N% of possibly money-having users. Are you actually advertising here?

This is precisely why several requirements were added to the PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) v 4.0 to make developers and deployers of payment pages inventory and authorize all the scripts that appear on the page, plus prevention of executing any authorized scripts. If payment card data was stolen, those authorizations are not occurring. PCI DSS Compliance is at risk for any of the sites that are not tracking this adequately. I’d strongly advise QSAs to investigate even more thoroughly exactly how this supply chain is monitiored and controlled.

And since EVERY PIC Compliant site now knows that this is a possibility, if I were still a QSA, I’d be asking in the next assessment for evidence of the Incident Response plan having been activated to ensure that no such breach had occurred on my assessed entity’s site, or the steps taken by the site to further stengthen their solution. IMHO there is no excuse for not having initiated an IRP by now.

It is a lot of work to use 3 browsers (Firefox, Mullvad, Tor), choose different VPNs and nodes and filter options, run them with multiple profiles, in different firejail options, on a machine with strict firewall settings, and in RAM to insure they are ephemeral. Eventually the Internet will be too much trouble.

I already spend more time thinking of ways to limit the damage than actually using the web. Now I’m off to figure out how to protect my brain…

People are surprised by this but the growing number of vulnerabilities over the past year have been crazy. AI has shown that it just gets better and better at finding and exploiting these vulnerabilities.

From Mythos at the beginning of the year being the scary held behind bars AI to Artex coming alive mid summer and exploiting everything it can.

The time to panic and fix was over months ago. This will probably get worse before the new year.
