#9668. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

#9666. Unity: Cannot set itself as MasterAtlas. Please assign a valid MasterAtlas.

Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at atlas-errors.petersoncool.workers.dev

In the Sprite Atlas Inspector, setting the Master Atlas field rejects your choice with Cannot set itself as MasterAtlas. Please assign a valid MasterAtlas. The field snaps back to its previous value, and the atlas you are editing keeps its current Type. If you opened the asset expecting it to behave as a variant that derives from another atlas, the variant relationship simply never takes effect, and sprites that should come through the scaled master keep resolving against whatever atlas was packed last.

A Variant Sprite Atlas does not hold its own packed texture at full size. It references a Master atlas and scales the master's contents down by its own Scale factor. The hierarchy only makes sense when the master is a different asset: a variant points up to a master, and the master packs the original sprites. When you drag the current atlas into its own Master Atlas field, you create a self-reference, a cycle where the variant would derive from itself. The inspector refuses that assignment on purpose, because a cycle cannot be resolved at pack time, and allowing it would leave the packer walking in circles looking for the texture source.

The same warning appears when the asset's Type was switched from Master to Variant after the field already held a reference, or when a copy-paste of an atlas asset carried the old master link along with it. It can also surface when two atlases in the project share the same name in your head but are actually the same file duplicated in the picker, so the target you select is still the asset you are editing. A related rejection covers the other direction of the same rule: assigning a second variant as the master is refused as well, because only a Master atlas may sit above a variant in the chain.

Open the atlas asset that raised the warning and read the Type dropdown at the top of the Inspector. If Type is set to Variant, the Master Atlas field must point to a different asset. Click that field and inspect the picker list: the entry that matches the current atlas's own name and file path is the one that triggered the self-reference. Cross-check the asset's file path against the master you intended, and confirm the two are separate .spriteatlas files under Assets.

A valid variant setup shows a Master Atlas entry whose file path differs from the current asset, and that master's own Type is Master. A broken setup either leaves the Master Atlas field empty after the rejected assignment, or holds a reference to the asset you are editing right now. If the project has only one atlas so far, that is usually the root cause: there is no second packed master for the variant to point at yet, and creating the variant before the master exists pushes you back onto the self-reference field.

Assign a real Master atlas that lives outside this asset:

If you meant for this asset to be the main packed atlas, switch Type back to Master instead of chasing the variant setup. A variant must always sit below its master in the hierarchy; it cannot be its own parent, and a second variant atlas cannot act as someone else's master either. When you duplicate an atlas to make a variant, re-check the Master Atlas field after the duplicate, because the copied reference can still point back to the original in a way that does not match the new asset's role.

After saving, reopen the Inspector and verify the Master Atlas path points to the other asset, Pack Preview succeeds without the warning, and sprites referenced through the variant load at the scaled size you expect. Check a scene that uses the variant directly, so the atlas resolves at runtime rather than only in the preview window.

The exact engine message and source location for this atlas warning are documented in the error reference.

#9663. De 15 minutos para 1 minuto: o script que gera os contratos do escritório onde trabalho

Trabalho num escritório de advocacia previdenciária desde janeiro e estou no 2º semestre de Engenharia de Software. Todo cliente novo precisa de um contrato, e quase todos passam pela minha mão: são de 10 a 15 por semana.

Fazer um contrato à mão levava uns 15 minutos. Abrir o modelo no Word, trocar nome, CPF, endereço e benefício, conferir tudo e mandar imprimir. Parece pouco, mas são de duas horas e meia a quase quatro horas por semana fazendo a mesma coisa, e cada digitação é uma chance de errar um número de CPF.

Hoje o mesmo contrato sai em cerca de 1 minuto. Vou contar como cheguei nisso, incluindo o que deu errado no caminho.

Minha primeira ideia foi pedir para a IA editar os documentos direto. Funcionou mais ou menos: chegou a levar 20 minutos para 3 documentos, mandou para a impressora errada e uma vez gerou um contrato com um dado faltando. Para um documento que o cliente vai assinar, "mais ou menos" não serve.

O que eu aprendi ali: para uma tarefa que se repete sempre igual, um script é melhor do que a IA. O script faz a mesma coisa toda vez. A IA, não.

Quando fui organizar os modelos, achei que eram 11 contratos diferentes, um para cada benefício. Olhando com calma, era um contrato só: o que mudava era o nome do benefício. E os outros documentos do kit (procuração, declarações) usavam o mesmo bloco com os dados do cliente.

Isso virou a base do projeto: um modelo, com marcadores no lugar dos dados ({{NOME}}, {{CPF}}, {{ENDERECO}}, {{BENEFICIO}}...), e um script que troca cada marcador pelo dado certo.

Eu não escrevi o código sozinho, e não escondo isso. O que fiz foi:

A IA continua no processo, mas só numa parte: ela me ajuda a reunir os dados da ficha. O texto do contrato vem sempre do modelo que os advogados aprovaram, nunca da IA.

E todo contrato ainda passa por uma pessoa antes de ser assinado.

O código e os modelos do escritório não podem ser públicos, porque envolvem dados de clientes. Então fiz uma demonstração com um modelo e um cliente fictícios, que roda direto no navegador e segue o mesmo caminho: ler a ficha, conferir os campos, abrir o modelo, trocar os marcadores e entregar o contrato.

Antes de pensar em ferramenta, vale olhar para o problema com calma. A descoberta de que eram um contrato só, e não onze, poupou mais trabalho do que qualquer linha de código. E usar IA para programar não tira a responsabilidade de quem publica: sou eu que testo, acho os erros e respondo pelo resultado.

Se você também trabalha num lugar cheio de tarefas repetitivas, comece anotando quanto tempo cada uma leva. É ali que estão os primeiros projetos.

#9661. LimeWire AI Studio Review 2023: Details, Pricing & Features

 

In the rapidly advancing landscape of AI technology and innovation, LimeWire emerges as a unique platform in the realm of generative AI tools. This platform not only stands out from the multitude of existing AI tools but also brings a fresh approach to content generation. LimeWire not only empowers users to create AI content but also provides creators with creative ways to share and monetize their creations.


As we explore LimeWire, our aim is to uncover its features, benefits for creators, and the exciting possibilities it offers for AI content generation. This platform presents an opportunity for users to harness the power of AI in image creation, all while enjoying the advantages of a free and accessible service.


Let's unravel the distinctive features that set LimeWire apart in the dynamic landscape of AI-powered tools, understanding how creators can leverage its capabilities to craft unique and engaging AI-generated images.


Introduction


LimeWire, a name once associated with the notorious file-sharing tool from the 2000s, has undergone a significant transformation. The LimeWire we discuss today is not the file-sharing application of the past but has re-emerged as an entirely new entity—a cutting-edge AI content publishing platform.

This revamped LimeWire invites users to register and unleash their creativity by crafting original AI content, which can then be shared and showcased on the LimeWire Studio. Notably, even acclaimed artists and musicians, such as Deadmau5, Soulja Boy, and Sean Kingston, have embraced this platform to publish their content in the form of NFT music, videos, and images.


Beyond providing a space for content creation and sharing, LimeWire introduces monetization models to empower users to earn revenue from their creations. This includes avenues such as earning ad revenue and participating in the burgeoning market of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs). As we delve further, we'll explore these monetization strategies in more detail to provide a comprehensive understanding of LimeWire's innovative approach to content creation and distribution.


LimeWire Studio welcomes content creators into its fold, providing a space to craft personalized AI-focused content for sharing with fans and followers. Within this creative hub, every piece of content generated becomes not just a creation but a unique asset—ownable and tradable. Fans have the opportunity to subscribe to creators' pages, immersing themselves in the creative journey and gaining ownership of digital collectibles that hold tradeable value within the LimeWire community. Notably, creators earn a 2.5% royalty each time their content is traded, adding a rewarding element to the creative process.


The platform's flexibility is evident in its content publication options. Creators can choose to share their work freely with the public or opt for a premium subscription model, granting exclusive access to specialized content for subscribers.


LimeWire AI Studio

As of the present moment, LimeWire focuses on AI Image Generation, offering a spectrum of creative possibilities to its user base. The platform, however, has ambitious plans on the horizon, aiming to broaden its offerings by introducing AI music and video generation tools in the near future. This strategic expansion promises creators even more avenues for expression and engagement with their audience, positioning LimeWire Studio as a dynamic and evolving platform within the realm of AI-powered content creation.


AI Image Generation Tools



The LimeWire AI image generation tool presents a versatile platform for both the creation and editing of images. Supporting advanced models such as Stable Diffusion 2.1, Stable Diffusion XL, and DALL-E 2, LimeWire offers a sophisticated toolkit for users to delve into the realm of generative AI art.


Much like other tools in the generative AI landscape, LimeWire provides a range of options catering to various levels of complexity in image creation. Users can initiate the creative process with prompts as simple as a few words or opt for more intricate instructions, tailoring the output to their artistic vision.


What sets LimeWire apart is its seamless integration of different AI models and design styles. Users have the flexibility to effortlessly switch between various AI models, exploring diverse design styles such as cinematic, digital art, pixel art, anime, analog film, and more. Each style imparts a distinctive visual identity to the generated AI art, enabling users to explore a broad spectrum of creative possibilities.


The platform also offers additional features, including samplers, allowing users to fine-tune the quality and detail levels of their creations. Customization options and prompt guidance further enhance the user experience, providing a user-friendly interface for both novice and experienced creators.


Excitingly, LimeWire is actively developing its proprietary AI model, signaling ongoing innovation and enhancements to its image generation capabilities. This upcoming addition holds the promise of further expanding the creative horizons for LimeWire users, making it an evolving and dynamic platform within the landscape of AI-driven art and image creation.

Sign Up Now To Get Free Credits

Automatically Mint Your Content As NFTs



Upon completing your creative endeavor on LimeWire, the platform allows you the option to publish your content. An intriguing feature follows this step: LimeWire automates the process of minting your creation as a Non-Fungible Token (NFT), utilizing either the Polygon or Algorand blockchain. This transformative step imbues your artwork with a unique digital signature, securing its authenticity and ownership in the decentralized realm.


Creators on LimeWire hold the power to decide the accessibility of their NFT creations. By opting for a public release, the content becomes discoverable by anyone, fostering a space for engagement and interaction. Furthermore, this choice opens the avenue for enthusiasts to trade the NFTs, adding a layer of community involvement to the artistic journey.


Alternatively, LimeWire acknowledges the importance of exclusivity. Creators can choose to share their posts exclusively with their premium subscribers. In doing so, the content remains a special offering solely for dedicated fans, creating an intimate and personalized experience within the LimeWire community. This flexibility in sharing options emphasizes LimeWire's commitment to empowering creators with choices in how they connect with their audience and distribute their digital creations.


After creating your content, you can choose to publish the content. It will automatically mint your creation as an NFT on the Polygon or Algorand blockchain. You can also choose whether to make it public or subscriber-only.


If you make it public, anyone can discover your content and even trade the NFTs. If you choose to share the post only with your premium subscribers, it will be exclusive only to your fans.


Earn Revenue From Your Content

Additionally, you can earn ad revenue from your content creations as well.

When you publish content on LimeWire, you will receive 70% of all ad revenue from other users who view your images, music, and videos on the platform.


This revenue model will be much more beneficial to designers. You can experiment with the AI image and content generation tools and share your creations while earning a small income on the side.


LMWR Tokens

The revenue you earn from your creations will come in the form of LMWR tokens, LimeWire’s own cryptocurrency.

Your earnings will be paid every month in LMWR, which you can then trade on many popular crypto exchange platforms like Kraken, ByBit, and UniSwap.

You can also use your LMWR tokens to pay for prompts when using LimeWire generative AI tools.

Pricing Plans

You can sign up to LimeWire to use its AI tools for free. You will receive 10 credits to use and generate up to 20 AI images per day. You will also receive 50% of the ad revenue share. However, you will get more benefits with premium plans.

  • Basic plan: 

For $9.99 per month, you will get 1,000 credits per month, up to 2 ,000 image generations, early access to new AI models, and 50% ad revenue share

  • Advanced plan: 

For $29 per month, you will get 3750 credits per month, up to 7500 image generations, early access to new AI models, and 60% ad revenue share

  • Pro plan: 

For $49 per month, you will get 5,000 credits per month, up to 10,000 image generations, early access to new AI models, and 70% ad revenue share

  • Pro Plus plan: 

For $99 per month, you will get 11,250 credits per month, up to 2 2,500 image generations, early access to new AI models, and 70% ad revenue share

With all premium plans, you will receive a Pro profile badge, full creation history, faster image generation, and no ads.

Sign Up Now To Get Free Credits

Conclusion

In conclusion, LimeWire emerges as a democratizing force in the creative landscape, providing an inclusive platform where anyone can unleash their artistic potential and effortlessly share their work. With the integration of AI, LimeWire eliminates traditional barriers, empowering designers, musicians, and artists to publish their creations and earn revenue with just a few clicks.


The ongoing commitment of LimeWire to innovation is evident in its plans to enhance generative AI tools with new features and models. The upcoming expansion to include music and video generation tools holds the promise of unlocking even more possibilities for creators. It sparks anticipation about the diverse and innovative ways in which artists will leverage these tools to produce and publish their own unique creations.


For those eager to explore, LimeWire's AI tools are readily accessible for free, providing an opportunity to experiment and delve into the world of generative art. As LimeWire continues to evolve, creators are encouraged to stay tuned for the launch of its forthcoming AI music and video generation tools, promising a future brimming with creative potential and endless artistic exploration

#9660. How Does a Fancy Text Generator Work Under the Hood?

How does a fancy text generator work under the hood? It swaps each plain letter for a different Unicode character that already looks bold, italic, script, or monospace. The Fancy Text Generator does this swap with a simple lookup table.

You type normal text, and the tool returns new text made from styled Unicode letters.

That swap is the whole trick. There is no font file attached to the output. There is no image hidden in the text.

The styled letters are plain text characters, just like A or B. That is why you can paste them into Instagram, WhatsApp, Discord, or a game chat. The app on the other end only needs to support Unicode text.

A font changes how a letter looks on screen. It does not change the letter itself. A fancy text generator does the opposite.

It changes the letter itself and leaves the font alone. The letter A becomes a different code point that was designed to look bold. The app then draws that new character with its normal font.

Think of it like a phone book for letters. The tool holds a table that pairs each plain letter with its styled twin. When you type D, the table returns the bold sans version.

When you type r, it returns the bold sans version of r. The tool repeats that step for every letter you type. Spaces and punctuation pass through with little or no change.

Here is what that swap looks like in practice. Plain text reads "Dream Big". The Bold Sans style returns "𝗗𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺 𝗕𝗶𝗴".

The Monospace style returns "𝙳𝚛𝚎𝚊𝚖 𝙱𝚒𝚐". The Fullwidth style returns "Ｄｒｅａｍ　Ｂｉｇ". Each version carries the same words.

Each version uses different characters under the surface.

That difference matters for developers. A font style is metadata that lives outside the text. A Unicode swap lives inside the text itself.

Once the swap is done, the style travels with the string. No style sheet follows it. No app needs to know that a style was applied.

Most styled letters come from one Unicode block. The block is called Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols. Its range is U+1D400 to U+1D7FF.

That range holds 1,024 code points. It was built for math notation, not for social media bios. Yet it holds exactly what a text styler needs.

Inside that block you will find bold serif letters, bold sans letters, italic serif letters, and bold italic letters. You will also find script letters, Fraktur letters, double-struck letters, monospace letters, and plain sans letters. Each set follows the same layout.

Uppercase A to Z comes first in each set. Lowercase a to z follows. Digits follow in some sets too.

The layout is regular by design. A developer can map plain A to bold A by adding a fixed offset. The same offset logic works for B, C, and the rest of the alphabet.

That regularity is why a generator can be built with a small table or a short bit of math. The tool does not need a huge database. It needs one clear rule per style.

Here is a concrete case from the live tool. The Bold Serif output for "Dream Big" is "𝐃𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐦 𝐁𝐢𝐠". The Script output for the same words is "𝒟𝓇ℯ𝒶𝓂 ℬ𝒾ℊ".

Both outputs spell the same phrase. Both come from the same block family. Only the chosen set changes.

A developer reading the raw text would see two different strings with the same meaning.

One detail deserves care. Not every style in the block is complete in the same way. Script has a few gaps where historic letters are used instead.

The tool handles those gaps in its table. A hand-built mapper that assumes a perfect grid will miss those cases. That is why a tested lookup table beats a clever offset formula in production.

Copy and paste works because the clipboard carries characters, not pixels. When you copy styled text, you copy a string of Unicode code points. When you paste it, the target app receives that same string.

It does not receive a font name or a style tag. It just draws the characters it was given.

That is why the same styled name can show up in a bio, a chat message, and a game lobby. Each app uses its own font to draw the text. Each font includes its own shapes for those Unicode characters.

The shapes may differ a little from app to app. The characters stay the same.

The system works best when the target font covers the block. Most modern fonts on phones and computers cover the common styled sets. Bold, italic, script, and monospace are widely supported.

Some rarer sets may fall back to a different font on an old device. The text still arrives intact. Only the drawing changes.

Search and storage work the same way. A database stores the styled string as text. A search box can hold it as text.

A screen reader will try to read it as text, though the result may sound odd. The key point stays simple. The style is data, not decoration.

It survives the trip because it is part of the string.

A basic generator needs three parts. First, it needs the input string from the user. Second, it needs a map from plain characters to styled characters.

Third, it needs an output step that joins the mapped characters back into one string. That is the core loop. Everything else is interface.

The map is the heart of the tool. For Bold Sans, plain D maps to one styled D. Plain r maps to one styled r.

The tool walks the input from left to right. It looks up each character in turn. If a character has a styled twin, it uses that twin.

If it has no twin, it keeps the plain character.

Most tools build one map per style. A tool with 36 styles holds 36 maps. That sounds like a lot of work, yet each map is short.

The alphabet has only 26 letters in each case. Digits add ten more slots. A small table can hold the whole set for one style.

You can test this idea with a short phrase. Type "Font Generator" into the tool and pick Bold Serif. The tool returns "𝐅𝐨𝐧𝐭 𝐆𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐫".

Type "Stylish Name" and pick Script. The tool returns "𝒮𝓉𝓎𝓁𝒾𝓈𝒽 𝒩𝒶𝓂ℯ". The words do not change.

A developer can build the same loop in any language. The steps stay the same in JavaScript, Python, or Go. Read the input.

Map each character. Join the result. The hard part is not the loop.

The hard part is getting the table right and testing it on real devices.

People often call the output a font. That word is handy, yet it is wrong in a technical sense. A font is a file that tells a system how to draw a character.

The styled text from a generator needs no such file. It uses characters that already exist in Unicode. The system draws them with whatever font is active.

This distinction explains a common surprise. You paste styled text into an app, and it looks different from the preview. The characters did not change.

The font did. The app drew the same code points with its own shapes. A real font change would travel as a setting.

The distinction also explains why the style survives a plain text file. Save styled text in a .txt file and reopen it later. The style is still there.

Save styled text in a font picker and change the font. The underlying characters stay styled. Fonts affect rendering.

For a developer, this is a useful mental model. Think of the generator as a translator between alphabets. It takes Latin letters and returns styled Latin letters.

It does not take a font and apply it. The output is still text, and any text pipeline can carry it.

Not every character has a styled twin. Numbers, punctuation, and symbols need their own rules. Some styles include styled digits.

Some styles leave digits plain. Some styles add marks above or below a letter instead of swapping it.

The strikethrough style is a good case. It does not swap letters at all. It adds a combining line after each letter.

The output for "Dream Big" is "D̶r̶e̶a̶m̶ B̶i̶g̶". Each base letter stays the same. A combining character follows it and draws a line through it.

Underline works the same way with a line below.

Wraps work in a different way again. A wrap style adds symbols around the whole phrase. The Stars Wrap output is "★ Dream Big ★".

The Hearts Wrap output is "♡ Dream Big ♡". The Crown Wrap output is "👑 Dream Big 👑". The inner words stay plain.

These edge cases show why a lookup table needs care. A swap style, a combining mark style, and a wrap style need different code paths. A single loop can still handle all three.

It just needs to know which path each style uses. A clean design keeps those paths apart so a fix in one style does not break another.

Styled text is fun, yet it has real limits. The first limit is support. Old systems may lack glyphs for some styled sets.

When a glyph is missing, the system shows a box or a question mark. The text is still valid. The display just cannot draw it.

The second limit is search. A search engine treats styled letters as different characters from plain letters. A search for plain "Dream Big" will not match "𝗗𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺 𝗕𝗶𝗴" as the same string.

That matters if the text needs to be found later. Use styled text for display. Use plain text for search, tags, and file names.

The third limit is access. Screen readers may read styled letters by their Unicode names. That can turn a short name into a long, confusing announcement.

A bio made only of styled text can be hard to use with assistive tech. Keep plain text nearby for key facts like a name or a link.

The fourth limit is length. Some styled characters take more bytes than plain letters. A name that fits in plain text may run long after styling.

Social apps with tight limits may cut the styled version short. Test the styled output in the target app before you rely on it.

The fifth limit is mixed styles. You can mix two styles in one phrase, yet the result can look messy. Each style has its own weight and spacing.

Bold Sans next to Script can clash. One style per phrase keeps the result clean. If you need contrast, change the words, not the style mid-phrase.

None of these limits break the tool. They just set where it fits best. Styled text works well for names, short bios, headings, and game tags.

It works less well for long posts, legal text, or anything that must be searched. Pick the job that fits the tool.

A quick check saves trouble later. Paste the styled text into the app where it will live. Look at it on a phone and on a desktop if you can.

Check that no boxes appear in place of letters. Check that the text still fits the field.

Try the decode step too. The Fancy Text Generator can turn styled text back into plain text. That reverse step is a good test.

If the tool can read the styled string and return plain "Dream Big", the mapping is clean. If it cannot, the string may hold a mixed set or a stray mark.

You can also compare styles side by side. The Fancy Text Examples page shows all 36 styles with the same sample words. That view makes it easy to spot a style that looks weak on your device.

Pick the style that reads well everywhere, not just in the preview.

A developer can go one step further. Copy the styled string into a code editor and inspect its length. A styled string may report more characters than the plain version.

That extra count comes from combining marks or wide characters. It is normal for some styles. It is worth knowing before the string hits a length limit.

A fancy text generator is a small program with a clear job. It maps plain letters to styled Unicode letters and returns the new string. The Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols block supplies most of the styled sets.

The clipboard carries the result because the result is text. No font file travels with it.

That simple design is why the tool feels fast. There is no rendering step on the server. There is no image to build.

The work is a lookup per character, repeated for a short string. The cost stays tiny even with 36 styles on offer.

If you build your own version, start with one style and one table. Test it with real words, not just the alphabet. Check the Script gaps.

Check digits and spaces. Check the result on a phone. Once one style is solid, the next 35 are the same pattern with new tables.

The charm of the tool is not magic. It is a neat reuse of a Unicode block that was built for math. A generator turns that block into a style picker.

You type plain words, and you get styled words back. The words stay words. Only the code points change.

#9659. Meet the Developer Advocate: Grigoriy Volgin on Building inDrive's Engineering Culture from the Inside Out

Byte off more tech news than you can chew, or die coding your own dreams.

Byte off more tech news than you can chew, or die coding your own dreams.

Meet Grigoriy Volgin, a Developer Relations specialist at inDrive based in Cyprus. In this installment of our Meet the Developer Advocate series, we explore DevRel philosophy, internal community growth, and the true meaning of developer experience. Grigoriy shares how inDrive—a global mobility platform that allows passengers and drivers to negotiate fair prices directly—cultivates a thriving, 600-strong internal engineering ecosystem.

I am Grigoriy Volgin, and I work in Developer Relations at inDrive, currently based in Cyprus. My role sits precisely at the intersection of engineering, communication, developer experience, and community building.

On a day-to-day basis, I help our engineers share their knowledge and build robust internal technical communities. This involves organizing conferences and hackathons, but it also means bringing our complex engineering stories to a global audience.

Another incredibly important part of my work is focused on improving the developer experience. It is essential to understand exactly what slows engineers down so we can help create an environment where they can focus purely on meaningful work.

inDrive is a global mobility and urban services platform. Unlike traditional ride-hailing platforms, inDrive allows passengers and drivers to agree on a fair price directly. Behind this relatively simple idea is a highly complex engineering ecosystem that operates across vastly different markets, cultures, and technological environments.

What I particularly enjoy about DevRel in this context is the ability to connect people, technology, and business. I strongly believe that a solid engineering culture is built not only through writing great code, but also through consistent knowledge sharing, deep trust, and cross-team collaboration.

For me, DevRel is a fluid mix of engineering, marketing, product, and community management. I would never limit it to just one of these areas. I think a highly effective DevRel specialist must fundamentally understand what engineers do on a daily basis, what specific problems they face, and what the company as a whole wants to achieve.

You do not necessarily need to be the absolute best engineer in the room, but you absolutely must speak the same language. Furthermore, I believe that authentic DevRel starts inside the company.

It is remarkably difficult to build a strong external developer community if you do not already have an active, engaged engineering community operating internally.

For me, this discipline is not just about organizing flashy events, publishing articles, or counting page views and social media likes. It is deeply rooted in building genuine relationships with engineers, understanding their core needs, and helping them solve real-world problems. Sometimes, something as simple as organizing a small internal meetup can bring far more tangible value to the team than sponsoring a massive external conference.

When it comes to acting as a bridge between the company and the engineers, I think everything comes down to trust. Developers should always feel entirely comfortable sharing their honest feedback with you, even when it is not something the company necessarily wants to hear.

For example, when we work on improving the Developer Experience at inDrive, I try to make sure that we remain focused on the actual problems our engineers face, rather than simply following our initial top-down assumptions.

Sometimes, this process requires actively questioning our own approach or respectfully suggesting different priorities based directly on the developer feedback we have gathered.

Of course, there are always strategic business priorities, strictly limited resources, and differing opinions across management. Not every single developer request can be implemented, and that is a completely normal part of software development.

For me, the most important thing is to maintain an open conversation flowing in both directions. You need to understand the overarching business goals, but you also need to be able to effectively translate and explain why certain technical or cultural things matter deeply to the engineering team.

At inDrive, we actively work with both internal and external engineering communities. Internally, our engineering community brings together around 600 people, including backend, mobile, frontend, QA, and platform engineers, as well as engineering managers operating from several different countries.

We maintain this ecosystem through regular technical meetups, dedicated sub-communities for different engineering disciplines, an internal Techleads Club, and regular hackathons.

Externally, we share our ongoing engineering experience with the broader industry through technical articles, conference speaking engagements, and public meetups. I think consistency is one of the main reasons our community has grown so successfully. You simply cannot organize one big event and expect to have a self-sustaining, active community immediately after that. It takes time.

Another crucial factor is giving our engineers more ownership over the community itself. We constantly encourage them to suggest their own topics, organize their own specialized meetups, and share their unique experiences.

As a DevRel specialist, my job is to act as a facilitator to support these initiatives, not to manage everything myself. In fact, some of our absolute best community activities started with a simple, direct message from an engineer who just wanted to share something interesting with their colleagues.

One of the projects I am most proud of is our recent internal hackathon at inDrive. It was our biggest hackathon so far, successfully bringing together people from different countries, disparate teams, and varying professional backgrounds into a single collaborative event.

We explicitly wanted to make it more than just a standard engineering competition. We structured it so that people could work on real business problems, experiment with new technologies, and develop creative ideas that they simply would not normally have the time to explore in their daily work.

Organizing a global hackathon is quite a logistical challenge. You have to navigate different time zones, coordinate across multiple office locations, manage online participants, and take care of a massive number of small operational details.

One of the biggest lessons I took away from this experience was that the work absolutely does not end when you announce the winners. It is equally important to help the participants continue to develop their ideas after the event concludes and to actively connect them with the right stakeholders.

For me, the ultimate best result of a hackathon is when people are so inspired that they want to continue working on their projects even after the formal competition is over.

At inDrive, we generally do not build software products specifically designed for external developers to consume, so my day-to-day experience is a bit different from a traditional SaaS DevRel role. However, we do maintain extensive internal platforms and tools where the exact same DevRel principles apply.

A fantastic recent example of this is our push for internal AI adoption. We realized early on that simply giving our engineers access to new AI tools was nowhere near enough. We needed to actively help them understand exactly how to incorporate these tools into their specific daily workflows.

To achieve this, we organized hands-on workshops, launched targeted educational programs, and highly encouraged our engineers to share their own personal experiences and practical use cases with the rest of the team.

The results were excellent. Between July and October 2026, the total number of AI tool users inside the company grew by almost 40 percent. Of course, this impressive growth was the result of several overlapping initiatives, not just DevRel.

But it proved to me that providing access to a piece of technology is only the first step. You also need to invest the time to help people understand what they can actually accomplish with it in practice.

When it comes to the content our team produces, one of my favorite recent articles is How We Scaled to 530 Aurora Clusters With a 4.5-Person DBA Team by Elizaveta Maznaya, our DBA team lead at inDrive.

It is a highly engaging story about how a remarkably small team managed to double its entire database infrastructure while simultaneously reducing the number of critical incidents from around 50 down to just eight in a six-month period.

What I really appreciate about this particular article is Liza's authentic writing style. She talks completely openly about her team's mistakes, their unsuccessful technical experiments, and the specific things she would do differently today.

The piece is packed with real production numbers, deep technical details, and even some well-placed humor. I think this exact combination is why this type of content works so well. It is clearly written by an engineer, specifically for other engineers, without trying to sell them anything.

As a DevRel specialist, my primary goal is to help our engineers maintain their own unique voice when we collaborate on technical content. I would much rather publish an article with a bit of genuine personality than a perfectly polished corporate success story.

Measuring the impact of DevRel can be tricky, but we track several distinct groups of metrics at inDrive to ensure we are moving in the right direction.

One of my absolute favorite metrics to watch is the number of unique engineers involved in internal knowledge sharing. It is incredibly important for me to see new speakers and first-time authors stepping forward, rather than just working with the same five people all the time.

I also make a point to look closely at what happens long after an activity concludes. Did a promising hackathon project actually move forward into production? Did engineers genuinely start using a new internal tool after attending a workshop?

I do not ignore basic metrics like likes, impressions, or event registrations, but I absolutely do not want to optimize our daily work for these numbers alone. They are useful indicators, but they do not always tell us how much actual value we have brought to the engineers.

When we sit down to prepare a technical article or draft a conference talk, I consistently encourage our engineers to include real-world examples, actual code snippets, detailed architecture diagrams, and hard numbers wherever possible.

It is also incredibly important to talk openly about our mistakes and transparently explain exactly why certain difficult decisions were made along the way.

The exact same principle applies heavily to our internal community efforts. For example, when we organize learning sessions about new AI tools, I heavily prefer live demos where engineers show exactly how they actually use these tools in their daily work, rather than presentations about the theoretical potential of AI.

Of course, not absolutely everything needs to include code. Sometimes, simply sharing an unsuccessful experiment or breaking down a difficult engineering decision can be just as valuable. My job in DevRel is to help our engineers share their experience, not to turn it into a marketing story.

There is a well-known saying that developers are allergic to marketing. I do not entirely agree with that premise. I think developers are not allergic to marketing itself; they just naturally reject marketing that brings them no value.

When we work on technical content at inDrive, I try to keep the final product as close as possible to the engineer's original story. We help with the structure, editing, and distribution, but the technical expertise and opinions should always come from the author.

I also firmly believe that engineers are the absolute best brand ambassadors a technology company could ever ask for. A developer authentically sharing their experience at a local meetup can sometimes do more for your tech brand than an expensive marketing campaign.

Another critically important aspect is choosing the right communication channels. You need to deeply understand where your audience spends their time, what they read, and what specific problems they are interested in solving.

Kathy Sierra argues that the primary goal is to make users awesome, rather than just making the product look awesome. That idea is foundational to how I approach my work.

I see Developer Relations as a specialized way to help our engineers grow professionally. We are here to help them become confident public speakers, to guide them as they publish their first technical articles, and to support them in building their own communities.

The exact same philosophy applies to Developer Experience. It is not about promoting internal tools, but about helping engineers do their complex jobs better and with less friction.

For me, a truly great result is when someone who once needed our DevRel support eventually steps up and starts actively helping other engineers grow alongside them.

Building a thriving engineering culture requires more than just deploying new tools; it requires deep trust, authentic communication, and a relentless focus on solving real developer problems. By prioritizing internal community building and practical knowledge sharing, Grigoriy Volgin and the team at inDrive prove that the most effective Developer Relations strategies start from the inside out.

Min Kim, Founder and CEO of SODAX, on the Future of Programmable Finance

#9658. Large Image Uploads in Node.js: Multipart, Sharp, and S3-Compatible Private Storage

Short answer: upload the original image with multipart, complete it before Sharp reads anything, and keep the source and thumbnails in separate private keys. That ordering protects large-file throughput and gives you a clean retry boundary; it does not, by itself, decide where pixels are processed or retained.

The tempting implementation is to pipe every incoming byte through the Node.js process and hand the stream to Sharp. It works on a laptop. It also turns your app into the slowest hop in the upload path, especially when a phone is sending a multi-hundred-megabyte video frame export over an unstable connection.

The experiment I would ship first is narrower: split the original into parts, upload those parts directly to object storage, and notify the backend only after the multipart upload is complete. The backend then downloads the completed object, runs Sharp, and writes derivatives under keys such as originals/{assetId} and thumbs/{assetId}/320.webp. A failed thumbnail job can be retried without touching the original.

There is one unglamorous cleanup task. Failed multipart sessions leave orphaned parts, so an abort path belongs in the job state machine; lifecycle rules do not automatically remove those fragments. Measure part retry rate, completion latency, Sharp processing time, and abandoned-upload bytes before choosing part sizes for your traffic.

The useful test is not a single successful upload. Put a 600 MB source on a throttled connection, kill the tab after part three, resume with the same asset id, and then inspect storage for both the completed original and the derivative keys. Repeat with a worker restart during Sharp processing. If the retry creates a second original, your key design is wrong; if it reads before completion, your queue contract is wrong; if deletion removes only the database row, your retention story is incomplete. Those checks expose trust and throughput failures together, which is why I prefer this experiment to a synthetic benchmark.

For a small team, Infrai fits the storage leg when you want discovery to explain the request and response shape before you write an adapter. That is a concrete fit for this pipeline, not a claim that it owns your image-processing or residency policy.

Treat the browser as an uploader, not a media processor. Your API creates an upload, returns presigned part URLs, and records an asset id. The client uploads parts with explicit retries, then the API completes the upload. Only a completed object enters the thumbnail queue.

Here is the small orchestration layer. The part upload itself uses the presigned URL returned by your storage adapter, so no application server has to proxy the bytes.

In production, make the idempotency key stable for the upload attempt rather than generating a new one on every process restart. Back off on 429 responses and honor Retry-After; a tight retry loop merely moves pressure to the storage boundary. The discovery document for each capability includes request and response schemas, which is useful when wiring this flow without learning a new SDK.

Private delivery means issuing a short-lived presigned URL for both the original and each thumbnail. It does not mean the object has a public ACL: this storage surface has no public-read mode and no permanent public URL. That makes it a poor fit for a static image host, but a sensible default for authenticated media in an app.

Region and processor choices remain explicit architecture decisions. If a provider must keep source images in a particular country, or a contract forbids sending pixels through a third-party processor, run Sharp inside that approved boundary and use storage only for the resulting object. A single API gateway cannot create a residency guarantee that your processor agreement does not contain.

Deletion needs the same discipline. Delete the original and derivatives as separate keys, record the operation in your database, and decide how long presigned links live. There is no object versioning or WORM lock here, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable by switching on a hidden flag. Strict concurrent writes need a queue or database lease because conditional If-Match writes are unavailable.

Infrai is worth trying for the storage part when a small team wants a self-describing HTTP interface: discovery exposes schemas and runnable examples, so adding a capability is an endpoint-reading exercise instead of another SDK integration. The supporting benefit is operational, not a price claim: one credential and billing surface can cover storage alongside other backend calls, while your Sharp worker remains ordinary Node.js code.

The catch is scope. Do not choose this layer for browser-direct uploads that require self-service CORS configuration, cross-region replication, object lock, or hourly lifecycle expiry. Stick with S3 when compliance needs those controls in one provider, choose R2 when its edge and egress model matches your users, and choose Spaces when a smaller operational surface matters more than governance depth. Your mileage may vary by region and contract; verify the processor list before moving real media.

Run a small canary with the largest images your product accepts. Confirm that a dropped client can resume parts, that an aborted session is explicitly cleaned up, and that a thumbnail job never reads a partial object. Check deletion with a real authenticated request, not just a database flag.

I started by treating “S3-compatible” as the whole answer. It isn’t. The throughput win comes from direct multipart transfer; the trust decision comes from region, retention, deletion, and who is allowed to process the bytes. Keep those decisions separate, and the pipeline stays replaceable.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the storage multipart discovery schema and test it against your own retention policy.

#9652. Why Scheduled Social Media Posts Fail to Publish (and How to Retry Safely)

Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at clienzo.co

Social media posts fail to publish more often than most schedulers let on. A post sits in the queue marked "scheduled", the time passes, and on one network nothing appears. Sometimes the tool tells you; often it does not, and the first sign is a client asking where Tuesday's post went.

This guide sorts the reasons a scheduled post fails into six causes, shows how to tell which one you hit, and gives the fix for each. It also covers the part people get wrong after the fix: retrying without posting twice on the networks that worked.

"Failed" is not one state. A post sent to five networks can land on four and be refused by one, and the four that worked must not be touched again. Before you change anything, collect three facts for each network the post was meant for:

If your scheduler shows a single status for the whole post, open each network and look. In Clienzo every network on a post shows its own result: a link to the live post, or the reason the network gave.

The most common cause. A scheduler publishes with permission the account owner granted, and that permission ends: the owner changed a password, removed the app in the network's settings, lost admin rights on a Page, or a token simply reached its expiry date. Meta, for example, documents that a long-lived user access token lasts about 60 days.

How to tell: every post to that one account fails, whatever its content, with a message about permissions, sessions or tokens.

Fix: reconnect the account from your scheduler, signing in as someone who still has the right role (Page admin, channel owner). For a client's account, ask the client to reconnect it or to give you the role again. Then check every other post scheduled to that account, because they would all have failed the same way.

Each network has its own rules for images and video: formats, file size, length, aspect ratio, how many images in one post. A video that is fine on YouTube can be too long for a Reel; a post with no image cannot go to Instagram at all.

How to tell: the error mentions the media, the format or the size, or the failure comes a few minutes after the scheduled time, once the network has tried to process the file.

Fix: check the network's own limits, re-export the file to fit, and give that network its own version of the post if the other networks are fine with the original. One cause that looks like a media problem but is not: the network could not download the file at all. A network fetches your image or video from a URL when it publishes; if that URL has expired or the host blocks the network's crawler, the post fails even though the file is perfect. We hit this ourselves when a robots.txt rule on a file host blocked Meta's fetcher, and Facebook video posts failed until the file was served another way.

Limits vary from 300 characters on Bluesky to thousands elsewhere, and networks count differently: some count bytes, some count every link as a fixed length. Our guide to character limits by network lists what each one counts.

How to tell: the network says the text is too long, or the post fails only on the network with the shortest limit.

Fix: shorten that network's version. A scheduler that checks each network's limit as you type catches this before the post is ever scheduled; Clienzo does, for each network a post goes to.

Some networks only let apps publish from certain accounts. Instagram's publishing API works with professional accounts (business or creator), not personal ones. On Facebook, apps publish to Pages, not to personal profiles.

How to tell: the account connected but every post to it fails, or the account never appears as a choice for the post.

Fix: switch the account type in the network's settings (for Instagram, to a professional account), then reconnect it.

Networks have outages, slow responses and rate limits. A post can fail with a generic server error and go through untouched an hour later. Two we have seen in practice: Threads answering "the requested resource does not exist" for a post it had just accepted, a few seconds before the post became available, and Bluesky returning an "UpstreamFailure" from the server that hosts an account.

How to tell: the message is vague (server error, timeout, upstream, try again later), the account and media are fine, and other posts to the same network work.

Fix: wait, then retry. Do not edit the post first: nothing in it was wrong.

Sometimes the network itself declines the post: a link it treats as spam, a duplicate of a post you just made, or content against its rules.

How to tell: the message mentions policy, spam, duplicates or a blocked link, and a retry fails the same way.

Fix: change what the network objected to (a different link, different wording) rather than retrying the same post.

Once the cause is fixed, the tempting move is to duplicate the post and schedule it again. If the post went out on some networks, that publishes it twice there, and a client will notice the double before you do.

Clienzo is built around knowing what happened to a post. Every network on every post shows a link to the live post or the reason it failed. A post that did not go out everywhere moves to the Failed tab with a badge on Posts, you get an alert in the app and an email, and you can have the same alerts in a Discord, Telegram or Slack channel. Retry sends only to the networks that failed, and when an account stops accepting Clienzo you are told before the next post is due. It is on every plan, Free included. More on post delivery tracking.

Originally published on the Clienzo blog.

#9651. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

Photography by Rick Holbrook; food styling by Kaitlin Wayne.

#9650. Switch between GPT and Claude in n8n without rebuilding your workflow

Disclosure: I work on ModelFold. The setup below follows the public ModelFold and n8n docs; I haven't run a paid request for this walkthrough.

If your automation needs a text response rather than an agent, you can compare two models with n8n's HTTP Request node. Keep the credential, endpoint, prompt, and downstream field fixed. Change just the model ID. Here's a small example: turn a synthetic support ticket into a one-line triage note.

Connect a Manual Trigger to an HTTP Request node. Choose POST and enter https://modelfold.ai/v1/chat/completions as the URL. That is the full endpoint, not the /v1 base URL used by SDKs.

Under Authentication, choose Generic Credential Type → Header Auth. In the credential, set Name to Authorization and Value to Bearer followed by your ModelFold API key. Keep the key in the credential, not in the JSON body or a screenshot.

Enable Send Body, choose JSON, select Using JSON, and paste:

Execute the node manually with a key you control. This sends a real request and may incur usage charges. Leave the response body unwrapped and read {{ $json.choices[0].message.content }} in the next node. Check for a missing or empty value before sending that output to another service; don't silently treat it as a successful summary.

Record the output, then change model to claude-sonnet-4-6 and rerun the same input. The response field stays the same. Ask two questions: Did the note preserve both facts (the export finished and the file was empty)? Did it avoid making up a cause? Use several sanitized tickets before swapping models in a live workflow. Compare actual outputs, not just whether a request returned successfully.

If the endpoint rejects a model ID, check the current ModelFold gateway docs and their model listing instructions. Use the spelling returned by the gateway. This walkthrough uses the complete JSON endpoint; it doesn't depend on streaming, function calling, or model-specific parameters.

Setup reference: n8n HTTP Request · n8n credentials · ModelFold API quickstart.

For a different question—whether AI assistants recommend your brand, rather than how to call them—see ModelFold GEO.

#9649. sqlite3_rsync：无需本地完整副本的 SQLite 远程复制

对于磁盘空间紧张的小型服务器，备份 SQLite 数据库时经常会遇到一个问题：数据库本身还放得下，但第二份完整副本已经放不下了。

sqlite3_rsync 提供了另一种选择：通过 SSH 将数据库快照复制到另一台机器，不必先在本地生成完整副本。

如果使用备份 API 或 VACUUM INTO 在本地创建数据库副本，就需要为这份副本预留足够的磁盘空间。当数据库已经占用磁盘容量的一半以上时，剩余空间可能不足以完成复制。

sqlite3_rsync 省去了先生成本地完整副本这一步，适合需要把数据库快照传到其他机器、但本地存储余量有限的场景。

对于写好标智库中关注数据库运维与工具选型的读者，这里值得区分的是两个问题：本地能否容纳完整副本，以及远程同步需要传输多少数据。sqlite3_rsync 分别从复制方式和差异比较机制上处理这两个问题。

除了复制快照，sqlite3_rsync 还可以同步已有的数据库副本。它采用与常规 rsync 类似的差异比较思路，以数据库页为单位识别需要传输的内容：

比较差异本身也有开销。如果两端数据库最初差异很大，交换哈希产生的额外流量，可能使总传输量超过完整数据库的大小，不过超出幅度最多约为几个百分点。

sqlite3_rsync 于 2024 年 10 月随 SQLite 3.47.0 以实验性工具的形式加入，并在 2025 年 5 月的 SQLite 3.50.0 中得到增强。

如果你的约束是“数据库还能运行，但磁盘已经容不下第二份完整副本”，这种复制方式值得纳入工具评估。

#9648. The Vitamin Deficiency Linked To Chronic Headaches

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Frequent headaches are linked to lower vitamin D levels.

People with chronic migraine have lower levels than those with occasional migraines or no headache disorder.

Lower vitamin D is also associated with greater muscle tenderness.

The vitamin helps muscles and nerves function, making it relevant to understanding pain.

One possibility is that low levels amplify sensitivity to pain, although this remains an explanation to investigate.

The research compared around 150 adults, divided equally between chronic migraine, episodic migraine and a group without headache disorders.

Blood tests showed low vitamin D in 78 percent of the chronic migraine group, compared with 60 percent of those with episodic migraine and 46 percent of the comparison group.

Average levels were lowest in chronic migraine and highest among those without headaches.

Chronic migraine means headaches on at least 15 days a month for more than three months, with migraine features on at least eight days.

These headaches can change in character, even within the same day, and can include pain resembling tension headaches.

Lower vitamin D levels were associated with more tenderness when muscles were pressed.

The researchers suggest that muscular discomfort and changes in pain processing could interact, potentially helping sustain headaches.

However, the association could also run in the opposite direction: people with migraine may spend less time outdoors because of light sensitivity or fatigue.

The findings do not establish that supplements prevent migraines.

Vitamin D’s established functions extend beyond maintaining strong bones.

It helps the body absorb calcium, supports muscle movement and allows nerves to carry messages between the brain and the body.

Deficiency can cause a condition called osteomalacia in adults, involving bone pain and muscle weakness.

The body produces vitamin D when sunlight reaches the skin, while food provides another source.

Oily fish, including salmon and mackerel, are among the best natural sources, while egg yolks contain smaller amounts.

Some breakfast cereals and other foods are fortified with the vitamin.

People who rarely expose their skin to sunlight can have more difficulty obtaining enough.

A blood test measures vitamin D status, helping distinguish a nutritional shortage from symptoms with other possible explanations.

The study was published in the journal Cephalalgia Reports (Prakash et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9647. The Immeasurable Value of Declarative Programming

The first is to tell the computer how to do something, step by step.

The second is to tell it what you want to hold true, and to write a common mechanism, which you build once, that applies what you told it.

The first is called imperative. The second is called declarative.

In imperative, you write the procedure yourself, every time.

In declarative, you describe the rule once, and the procedure is executed every time by the mechanism you wrote.

We all started with the first, the imperative way. It is the natural way. You write code that says: take this, put it there, check this, save the other.

And for small programs, it works wonderfully.

The problem begins when the program grows. When you go from 5 tables to 50. From 1 form to 200. From 1 developer to a team.

Then the "how" starts to repeat itself. The same thing, written again and again, in a thousand places, with small differences that nobody remembers why they exist.

That is where declarative shows its value. And its value is not small. It is immeasurable.

Declarative does not mean "without code". It means "code that describes".

Take the Product, take its price, put it in the Line, take its name, put it in the Line, take its VAT rate, put it in the Line...

The Order Line has a lookup to the Product. When a Product is selected, the fields Name, Price, VAT Rate are copied.

The first version is instructions. The second is a definition.

The definition is written once. And it is executed every time, by the framework, automatically, in the same way, without errors, without omissions.

That is the difference. It is not syntactic. It is architectural.

And there is something else, which is the key: a declarative definition is not just code that runs. It is knowledge that the system can use.

The copy mechanism uses it. The UI uses it. Validation uses it. Any code in your application can use it.

Nobody needs to discover inside the code what you meant. The system knows it. Because you told it once, clearly.

Let us take the most classic example from business applications: the Order.

We have a Customer, an Item, an Order and its Lines.

When the user creates an Order, they select a Customer and an Item. At that moment, we must keep a snapshot of the state as it was then.

Why? Because tomorrow the Customer may change their company name. They may change their billing address. They may change their shipping address. The Item may change its price. It may change its description. It may change its VAT rate.

The Order, however, must not change. The Order is a historical document. It must remember how the world was at the moment it was issued.

And for anyone who has built an ERP, CRM, accounting system, warehouse system, it is an obvious need that they exist and are kept up to date.

It is defined nowhere. Or rather, it is defined everywhere.

It is defined in the Service that creates the Order. It is defined in the Service that processes it. It is defined in the API that accepts it. It is defined in the form that shows it. It is defined in the import that brings it in from elsewhere.

Take the name from the Item, put it in the Line. Take the price from the Item, put it in the Line.

And if tomorrow we must also keep something else, for example the Item's barcode as it was then, we must find all these places and change them one by one.

It is defined once, in the definition of the lookup.

The field ProductId of the Line is a lookup to the Product table. When it changes, the following fields are copied: Product.Name -> OrderLine.ProductName Product.Price -> OrderLine.Price Product.VatRate -> OrderLine.VatRate Product.Barcode -> OrderLine.Barcode

And in code, the same definition may look something like this. The example is indicative, it does not belong to a specific library:

From then on, whoever creates an Order, from wherever they create it, from a form, from an API, from an import, from an automatic process, the snapshot will happen automatically, in the same way.

And if tomorrow we must add the barcode, we add it in one place: in the definition. Not in a thousand.

That is the difference between "we know it" and "we have defined it".

Copying fields is a mechanism. Which data we keep and when we change it is a business decision. A declarative definition lets us express our knowledge in a concentrated way.

Let us take the second example, which is perhaps even more revealing.

Suppose we have a system that works. It has 50 tables, 200 forms, 100 reports.

And the Customer comes and says: "I want to add the field 'Profession' to the Customer".

What needs to happen in the imperative approach?

Twelve places for one field. And if you forget one, the system works, but something is missing. And nobody notices immediately.

And if the field is a lookup, for example "Profession" selected from a list, multiply the above by two, because you must also build the lookup, and the snapshot, and the lookup's form.

Now imagine it is not one field, but an entire table. Or ten tables. Or an entire module.

You add the field to the definition of the table.

Table Customer, field Profession, type string, length 100, required no, visible yes.

The form shows it automatically, because it is built from the definition. The grid shows it automatically, because it is built from the definition. The filter has it automatically. Validation does it automatically. The API exposes it automatically. The export has it automatically.

You did not write the same thing twelve times. You wrote it once, and the system understood it.

The application knows what the field is. Let it use that knowledge.

That does not mean that every field is necessarily shown everywhere. It may be hidden in the grid, available only to certain user roles, excluded from the public API. But those too are pieces of information expressed declaratively, in the same definition. They are not code scattered across 12 files.

In business applications, 80% of forms are the same: a header with fields, a grid with lines, some lookups, some Insert / Edit / Delete / Save buttons.

In the imperative approach, you build the same form 200 times, with small differences. And every time you write:

Make a TextBox for the Name. Make a TextBox for the Address. Make a Lookup for the Customer. Make a Grid for the Lines.

In the declarative approach, you do not build a form. You define that the Order table has a form, and the form is built from the definition of the table.

If you want something custom, you make it custom. But the 80% that is standard, you do not rewrite it.

This has two consequences that are not immediately visible.

The first is speed. You can build an entire application in days, not months.

The second, which is more important, is consistency. All forms work the same way. The user learns once how the Lookup works, and knows how it works everywhere. The developer learns once how the framework works, and knows how it works everywhere.

In the imperative approach, every form is a small, different program. With its own bugs. With its own quirks.

And yes, in the declarative approach, a bug in the common mechanism will affect many forms. But I prefer a thousand times to fix a bug in one place, than to chase two hundred variations of the same bug in two hundred forms.

The answer is that declarative is harder at the beginning. Much harder.

To say "I define the table and the form builds itself", you must first build the mechanism that builds forms from definitions. You must build the mechanism that does snapshots. You must build the mechanism that does lookups, locators, filters, validations, code providers.

You end up building a framework. And building a framework is much harder than building an application.

That is why most developers, and most teams, choose the imperative road. Because it is direct. You write code, you see results. You do not need to design anything in advance.

And for a small application, they are right. It is faster.

For a large application, that will live for 10 years, that will keep changing, that will be maintained by people who did not write it, the imperative road slowly becomes unmaintainable. Not because the developers are bad. But because the knowledge is scattered in a thousand places, and nobody knows where it all is.

Declarative is an investment. You pay at the beginning, you gain continuously.

And no, not every team needs to build its own framework. And no, not every small application justifies such an investment.

But at some point we must stop measuring only how fast we wrote the first form.

Declarative does not mean "without code". It does not mean "low-code". It does not mean "drag and drop".

Declarative means that your code describes what holds true, not how it will happen.

You can write declarative code in C#, in Java, in TypeScript, in any language. The language does not matter. The mindset does.

And declarative does not mean that you never write imperative code. Of course you do. When you have a complex calculation, a complex rule, a complex flow, you will write imperative code. And you will do well.

The difference is: where do you put the imperative?

You put it where there is real business logic. Not where there is repetition.

The snapshot is not business logic. It is a mechanism. You should not write it every time.

The form is not business logic. It is presentation. You should not rebuild it every time.

The business logic is: "If the Customer is wholesale, the discount is 10%, otherwise 0%". You write that once, in code, and it is right that it is imperative.

And let us make one more thing clear. Abstraction does not replace knowledge.

If a tool generates SQL, that does not mean you do not need to understand databases and SQL. If a framework generates forms, that does not mean you do not need to understand UI. If it copies snapshot fields, someone must have correctly decided what those snapshots mean.

Good infrastructure executes the knowledge we gave it. It does not fix our ignorance.

The value of declarative does not show in the first week. It shows in the first year. And in the fifth. And in the tenth.

It is not about language. It is not about framework. It is not about Java or .NET, Entity Framework or Hibernate.

It is a matter of decision: Will we define once what holds true, or will we rewrite it every time?

Whoever chooses declarative, pays at the beginning. And gains forever.

Whoever chooses imperative, gains at the beginning. And pays forever.
