#9628. The Simple Drink Swap Linked To 41% More Weight Loss

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.

Women with type 2 diabetes who make the switch lose around 41 percent more weight over 18 months than those who continue drinking diet beverages.

They are also twice as likely to achieve diabetes remission during a structured weight-management programme.

The findings raise a question about whether a drink’s calorie count tells the whole story about its effects on weight.

Sweet taste without the accompanying energy might influence appetite signals.

The results suggest that everyday drink choices could play a useful supporting role in longer-term weight management.

The research involved around 80 women who were overweight or had obesity, had type 2 diabetes and regularly consumed diet drinks.

Researchers randomly assigned them either to replace their usual diet beverage with water after lunch five times a week or to continue drinking it.

Both groups took part in a six-month weight-loss programme followed by a year devoted to maintaining their progress.

By the end, women assigned to water had lost an average of 6.82 kg, compared with 4.85 kg among those continuing with diet drinks.

The difference amounted to almost 2 kg of additional weight loss across the programme.

The water group also showed greater improvements in measures including fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance and blood fats.

Diabetes remission was reported in 90 percent of women assigned to water, compared with 45 percent of those continuing diet beverages.

Dr Hamid R. Farshchi, study co-author, said:

“It’s a small change with the potential for a big impact on long-term health outcomes.”

The brain may respond differently when a sweet taste arrives without the energy normally supplied by sugar.

In a separate experiment involving around 75 adults, participants reported greater hunger after consuming sucralose than sugar, and the sweetener altered activity in the hypothalamus, a brain region involved in appetite regulation (Chakravartti et al., 2025).

However, hunger ratings after sucralose did not differ from those after water, so the findings do not establish that sweetened drinks necessarily make people hungrier than plain water.

The mismatch between sweetness and energy might help explain some appetite responses, but whether it contributed to the weight-loss difference remains unknown.

The study was published in the journal Diabetes (Farshchi Nasr et al., 2025).

#9621. Aggressive Policing as a Public Health Issue

The medical field has paid increased attention to the negative health impacts of systemic racism, discrimination, poverty, and other societal forces that are known to cause poorer health. This includes awareness of the need to assess and address racial and other health disparities and focus on principles of diversity, equity, and inclusion. We have moved beyond the framing of these issues as moral imperatives to understanding how they are related to individual and public health.

Discussion of the health harms of aggressive policing has also increased over the last 2 years, spurred by the frequent and well-publicized deaths of Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC). What has been viewed as a political issue is now understood as a public health/health inequity concern. Two articles that have helped change the way the medical community views these issues were published in 2021:

Both of these pieces help illustrate the ongoing shift in how police violence and aggressive policing have specific and disproportionate impacts on communities of color.

The first article makes several key points in its assertion that policing concerns should be viewed as health issues. It begins with this statement:

“Marginalized communities have a long history of naming the systemic racism and harms of police violence to health and well-being and recognizing their roots in the oppression of Black and Indigenous communities.”

The article cites data indicating that BIPOC are far more likely to be killed by police than White Americans, noting that death at the hands of a police officer is the sixth leading cause of death for young Black men. Similarly, Black and Indigenous women are more likely to be killed by a police officer than their White counterparts.

The second article also looks at specific data related to the disparate impact of what is describes as the “overexposure” to aggressive policing strategies among Black communities, serving to increase already existing health disparities in such communities. The article authors noted:

“Indeed, aggressive policing strategies employed by law enforcement agencies across the country have been hypothesized to degrade health and well-being, even among people who themselves have not experienced contact with police. Perhaps even more important, aggressive policing is thought to contribute to significant population health inequities, as these practices are concentrated on — and thus exacerbate — the health challenges faced by racialized populations.”

The authors of the article cited data from an organization called Campaign Zero.3 This group’s website includes data that also helps demonstrated the negative impact of aggressive policing, or what they describe as “broken windows” policing. This form of policing has led to the overpolicing of communities of color with resulting excessive force, leading to unnecessary deaths.

“Meanwhile, the vast majority of arrests are for low-level, nonviolent activities in encounters that often escalate to deadly force. For example, in 2014, police killed at least 287 people who were involved in minor offenses and harmless activities like sleeping in parks, possessing drugs, looking “suspicious” or having a mental health crisis. These activities are often symptoms of underlying issues of drug addiction, homelessness, and mental illness, which should be treated by health care professionals and social workers rather than the police.”

These 3 examples of the evolving understanding of how to view police aggressiveness highlight the need for future research and data collection. They also highlight the need for PAs, nurse practitioners, and other medical providers to assess the health impact of high-impact policing on their patients and to advocate for changes to a policing system that results in furthering existing health disparities.

1. Fleming PJ, Lopez WD, Spolum M, Anderson RE, Reyes AG, Schulz AJ. Policing is a public health issue: the important role of health educators. Health Educ Behav. 2021:10901981211001010. doi:10.1177/10901981211001010

2. Esposito M, Larimore S, Lee H. Aggressive policing, health, and health equity. Health Policy Brief. Health Affairs. April 30, 2021. doi:10.1377/hpb20210412.997570.

3. Campaign Zero. https://www.joincampaignzero.org/solutions#solutionsoverview

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.

#9617. Not Mayo Or Butter: Grilled Cheese Is Even Tastier With One Creamy Store-Bought Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

A classic grilled cheese is a thing of both beauty and comfort. And of course, a simple sandwich such as this is open to interpretation, with many putting their own spin on it, like making it Swiss-style with raclette cheese or switching up the grilling process by using an air fryer, like Ree Drummond. But there's an easy addition you can make to your next grilled cheese that will make it even tastier (and it's not mayo or butter, though you can certainly use either): It's store-bought caramelized onion dip.

When spread onto the bread and covered in cheese, then warmed through in a hot pan, caramelized onion dip brings a burst of flavor and a compelling texture to the sandwich. Of course, it's definitely savory, but the caramelized onions also introduce a subtly sweet element to grilled cheese, creating a flavor sensation that is much more interesting for your taste buds. Meanwhile, the dip melts into the cheese, adding to the creaminess, while the onions introduce a little toothsome variety to chew on, beyond the softness of the filling and the crispness of the bread.

Trader Joe's Caramelized Onion Dip is one great store-bought option, and it's part of the store's regular lineup, so you should be able to find it year-round (unless it has sold out). Whole Foods also sells a version under its 365 brand, which Amazon Prime members can shop for on Amazon.

If you have the desire to take things a step further, you might try a mix-in or two that can elevate the taste of the dip (and therefore, your entire sandwich). That might include some dried cranberries, which can help draw out the aforementioned sweetness of the onions, creating an even bolder contrast in your salty grilled cheese. You also might play to the richness and crumble up some crisp bacon into the base. Or enhance the savory, aromatic vibes by adding both thinly sliced scallions and chives.

Now, if you're having trouble finding caramelized onion dip at your grocery store, you could always make your own, though cooking down the onions properly can be laborious. If standing over your stove for 45 minutes doesn't appeal to you, Ina Garten cuts down on the time by using a larger pot, which allows the onions to cook more evenly and efficiently. But if you'd rather skip the cooking altogether, you might find the adjacent caramelized onion jam on store shelves. This won't be as creamy as the dip, but it will still impart that same rich, savory, and slightly sweet flavor, so it's a decent substitution.

#9614. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

Cover photo by Mark Weinberg; food styling by Liz Neily.

#9609. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

#9605. Add This Creamy Ingredient To Ground Beef For A Juicier Burger With Extra Protein

Incorporating secret ingredients into your burger patties elevates the dish in unexpected ways. Some components flavor the meat while others enhance the texture. For an add-in that does both — with a delicious underlying creaminess — look no further than yogurt. The dairy works as a ground beef tenderizer, making a burger that's softer and full of moisture. Not to mention, yogurt is an effective enhancement in chicken or turkey patties, too.

Yogurt's contained lactic acid functions as a mild, but nevertheless efficient, tenderizer, lightly marinating the meat. The inclusion of a liquid naturally adds lots of moisture to a burger — you certainly won't have to worry about a disappointingly dry result. Plus, the ingredient lends the burger a lightly creamy mouthfeel.

And if you use Greek yogurt for the task, you'll get a nice dose of added protein, too. Mix in a quarter cup of whole milk Greek yogurt — a quantity suitable for a pound of meat — and you'll up the dish by 5.5 grams of protein. This yogurt's extra fat content will further prevent dryness, all while forming a patty that's not too loose, making a burger rendition that stands out.

Working yogurt into your beef patties doesn't require any special technique. You can simply stir the dairy with the beef in a bowl, seasoning with salt and pepper in parallel. Follow by forming the patties as usual, then lightly brush the exterior with oil to prevent unwanted adhesion. Prepare the yogurt burgers using your preferred method, whether you're fond of using a skillet or grilling burgers like a pro. However, if you notice your mixture appears too wet, consider adding a binder — chia seeds are a fantastic option to absorb moisture but keep things tender and juicy; panko breadcrumbs will also absorb excess liquid while keeping the bite of each burger soft.

Such a burger tastes delicious with classic seasonings, but don't rule out creative modifications, too. The pairing of yogurt and beef recalls Greek and Middle Eastern cuisine, so consider integrating Eastern Mediterranean seasonings into the build.

A Greek burger spin could fold in oregano, lemon, and feta — core flavors of a Greek salad. A kofta-style patty might up the spice, working in earthy cumin, a dash of spicy harissa, and grated garlic into the mix. Alternatively, season the meat in a sweet direction by using simply turmeric and onions; the ingredients will set you up for a wide array of flavorful condiments. Build out the meal with an aromatic herbal yogurt sauce, a bold dose of roasted peppers, or a marinated arugula salad, and you'll make a burger rendition that'll become a frequent part of the rotation.

#9602. Give Canned Baked Beans A Delicious Upgrade With A Drizzle Of This Ingredient (Hint: It's Not Honey)

When you need a side to go along with your main dinner entree and you need one fast, it's reassuring to know that shelf-stable, pantry-sitting canned goods have got your back. Included in Food Republic's list of inexpensive canned foods you'll use all the time are beans, and along with the plain black or red varieties (which typically need to be combined with other ingredients to make a reasonable side), you could also reach for scrumptious, creamy baked beans. But while they're totally fine heated up straight from the can, they can certainly benefit from a drizzle of molasses.

Molasses might not be the first thing you think of when you consider add-ins, but many homemade recipes call for it, and for good reason. Made by boiling down sugarcane juice or refining sugar, the rich, thick syrup is slightly smoky and sweet, with robust, burnt caramel notes, making it a perfect match for deepening the flavor of sometimes weak-tasting canned baked beans and bringing them closer to homemade.

It is for this reason that molasses is also preferable to honey here. Honey is intensely sweet, can taste almost floral at times, and has a delicate flavor, whereas molasses is bolder and has a meatier taste that can make its presence known among the other ingredients in the dish.

It's important to note that there are three main types of molasses: light, dark, and blackstrap, and they each have different flavor profiles. For canned baked beans, you'll likely want to stick with light or dark because blackstrap is intensely bitter (also, light is the sweetest of the three, so if sweetness is important to you, go with that one). If you're heating the beans on the stove, you can start by drizzling in about half a tablespoon of molasses per 28-ounce can, bringing the mixture to a boil, and then simmering for about 10 minutes. If you're baking them, likewise, just stir in the molasses before putting the dish in the oven — it couldn't be simpler.

If you don't have any molasses sitting about, don't panic. There are plenty of other additions that can help upgrade canned baked beans and make them taste less, well, pantry-fied. Take brown sugar, for example — did you know that it's often just white sugar and molasses combined? A little bit will still bring that sweet contrast to balance out the savory flavors and give you a deeper, more complex finish.

Another great option is one you might normally use on your pancakes: maple syrup. You don't want to use the fake stuff that's primarily made of corn syrup and artificial flavors and colors, but rather 100% real Grade A maple syrup for the best flavor. Its sweetness again deliciously contrasts with and enhances the canned baked beans' savoriness, while the maple flavor adds its unique caramelly, toffee-like notes to the dish.

#9599. Make Your Next Breakfast Sandwich Korean-Style For A Major Fiber & Flavor Boost

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Think of Korean cuisine, and a sandwich likely isn't the first thing that comes to mind. However, bread-based dishes are widely enjoyed in the East Asian country, both in cafes and as street food. An especially popular breakfast rendition is gilgeori toast, a comforting breakfast sandwich stuffed with eggs and shredded vegetables.

Easy-to-make, packed with fiber, and delicious, the dish is a great candidate for your breakfast rotation. Traditionally, this sandwich calls for a fluffy loaf of milk or brioche bread, the buttery soft texture turning crisp on the outside once toasted. Meanwhile, the filling comprises a variable shredded vegetable medley: Cabbage traditionally forms the centerpiece, joined by carrots, onions, scallions, and often garlic chives. Mixed with egg and then pan-fried into an aesthetic golden-brown patty, the filling delectably complements the soft bread. Gilgeori is usually rounded out with a sprinkle of sugar and a drizzle of ketchup and mustard.

It's an assembly that easily comes together during bleary morning hours, yet nevertheless offers a nutritious start to the day. One sandwich can pack in around six ounces of shredded cabbage, which amounts to over 4 grams of fiber. Add up the fiber from a tablespoon of carrot, two of sliced onion, and two whole green onions, and you're including another 1.5 grams. Then, add in two slices of thick-cut brioche sandwich bread, and you've got an extra 2. That's about 7.5 grams, which is around a quarter of what you need a day, already knocked out by breakfast. Mixed with the roughly 6.5 grams of protein from the egg alongside filling bread, the sandwich serves as a terrific way to start the day.

The morning isn't always the best time to precisely reconstruct a recipe. Thankfully, gilgeori toast welcomes a wide array of reinterpretations and ingredients. Starting with the bread, feel free to swap the milk bread for sourdough, whole wheat, or even a convenient store-bought whole grain like Ezekiel or Dave's Killer. You'll lose out on some of the dish's airiness, but potentially gain extra fiber content in the process. Two slices of Dave's Killer 21 Whole Grains and Seeds contain some 8 grams of fiber, more than doubling the total of the sandwich.

Up the satiation further by adding on a slice of seared ham, a filling also enjoyed in Korea. And cheese is always welcome, whether American, cheddar, or fontina – Martha Stewart's go-to for breakfast sandwiches. Instead of the sugar sprinkle, lend the dish a sweet note by using jam: Raspberry or cherry jam makes a great fit. Not to mention, you can replace the ketchup and mustard with a condiment of your preference; you can buy a bottle of Gochujang Sriracha Hot Sauce online, for instance. The template of bread and shredded vegetables works with many flavors, perfect for morning enjoyment.

#9598. What Couples Married For 40 Years Do When Life Gets Hard

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.

They describe listening to each other, talking through painful subjects and sometimes having the same argument more than once.

The researchers suggest that this response grows out of years of knowing they can count on their partner.

In attachment theory, a partner can act as a safe haven, someone whose presence makes it easier to bear distress.

Getting through a difficult period together may deepen that trust, making it easier to ask for help the next time it is needed.

Dr Christian Heim, the study’s first author, and Dr Caroline Heim, study co-author, interviewed each couple together, asking each person to describe what had put their marriage under strain and what had helped them cope.

The 180 participants were born in 24 countries and, with a few exceptions, had been married for at least 40 years.

Around two-thirds of the couples described a threat they believed could have ended their marriage, such as the death or serious illness of a child, infidelity or prolonged periods apart.

Talking, listening and arguing accounted for almost a quarter of the coping responses the researchers recorded.

After an affair, some couples described arguing over it repeatedly, while bereaved partners sometimes waited for a moment when both felt able to speak.

One partner in an American couple married for 45 years recalled asking their spouse about the son they had lost.

“Can I talk about our son? I’m hurting. Is it okay to talk about it?”

Some partners described taking time to grieve separately before they were ready to turn to each other.

Around four in five coping responses involved leaning on the relationship, whether by drawing closer, persevering as a couple or giving up something one partner wanted.

The interviews capture what couples in lasting marriages felt had helped them, leaving open whether the same approaches would have helped couples who separated.

When partners see a problem as something they face together, they may spend less time working out who is to blame and more time trying to understand what the other person is going through.

A previous analysis involving almost 18,000 people found that coping together and helping a partner manage stress were both linked to greater relationship satisfaction (Falconier et al., 2015).

Some couples in the interviews felt that an illness, a bereavement or a family conflict had left them closer, even though the experience itself had been painful.

A British couple married for 60 years described how they got through a serious conflict with their in-laws:

The study was published in the journal The American Journal of Family Therapy (Heim & Heim, 2025).

#9595. COVID-19 and Moral Injury: a Mental Health Pandemic for Frontline Health Care Workers

More than 2 years ago, the alarm and first warnings of a global pandemic sounded. Now with over 830,000 deaths caused by COVID-19 in the US, there looms on the horizon a second underlying curve with equally serious long-term consequences: a mental health pandemic.

The mental health fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic demands recognition, intervention, and mitigation strategies. Among the many at-risk populations are frontline health care workers who have been at the epicenter of the global pandemic, working long shifts with at times a tenuous safety net and limited support, and caring for COVID-19 patients with limited resources, mixed messaging, and uncertainty with regards to an end to the crisis. The psychological effects in some health care providers are akin to the moral trauma or moral injury that is recognized in combat veterans with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Mental health professionals and other health care providers caring for frontline health care workers who present with insomnia, depression, anxiety, panic attacks, PTSD, and suicidal thoughts should recognize and validate their experiences and moral injury. Intervention strategies including health promotion, resilience training, and ongoing multilevel support will play an important role in flattening the moral injury curve.

As a rule, the frontline health care workforce is considered capable, competent, resilient, professional, and persevering in the face of adversity. However, COVID-19 presented as an unprecedented crisis unlike any other unforeseen disaster, eliciting fear, uncertainty, and anxiety, coupled with grief and loss, both personally and professionally.1 As noted by Warren D. Taylor, MD, MHSc, and Jennifer Urbano Blackford, PhD1:

The pandemic created anxiety and fear in health care providers, from physicians and nurses to allied health professionals and first-line responders. We fear for the safety of our families and patients. We grieve for those who have died. We feel guilt for not being able to save all our patients, for getting sick ourselves, and for abandoning our families. Many adopted the phrase, “we will get through this together but none of us will survive unscathed.”

At the outset, the shortage of equipment and resources, changing practice guidelines, and unpredictability of the workload rendered health care workers with a sense of powerlessness and loss of control of the conditions under which they were able to deliver care. The emotional distress and social isolation from family and friends exacted an immeasurable toll on the physical health and emotional well-being of the workforce, setting the stage for the inevitable moral injury.2

Moral injury is a term that has been applied to veterans of combat. Moral injury or moral distress as experienced by frontline health care providers occurs when health care providers are forced to make decisions that transgress their professional commitment to patient comfort and care, and forcibly shift their moral compass. They are not able to meet the physical, emotional, and end-of-life needs of patients.3

Watson et al noted that moral injury in health care workers “can occur when someone engages in, fails to prevent, or witnesses acts that conflict with their values or beliefs.”4 Moral injuries may result from the following, according to Watson et al4:

The consequences of such experiences may include feelings of rage, guilt, shame, and anger and moral injury is the “lasting psychological, spiritual, behavioral or social impact that may result from these experiences.”4 The number of acutely ill COVID-19 patients and high death rate coupled with lack of resources and at times rationing of limited resources such as personal protective equipment (PPE) and ventilators added to the dilemma that frontline health care workers faced.

In a study of 448 Jordanian nurses during the COVID-19 pandemic, the majority of nurses (64%) reported experiencing acute stress disorder (ASD) and 41% reported significant psychological distress, with a predilection for younger nurses compared to older nurses.5 However, coping self-efficacy was a protective factor with the potential to mitigate the severity of psychological distress.5 An online survey of nonhealth care providers (N=976) found that individuals with previous trauma were at highest risk for increased symptoms of anxiety, depression, and PTSD related to COVID-19 compared with individuals with no previous history of trauma.6

The long-term mental health consequences of moral injury for frontline health care workers have important implications for workforce survivability and durability; however, research on this topic is lacking. In one of the few published studies on moral injury among health care providers, investigators looked at the thematic content of experiences reported by nurses following incidents meeting the contextual definition of moral injury (ie, events with unintended consequences, potentially causing patient harm or putting patients at risk for serious injury). The investigators found nurses reported experiencing “guilt, shame, spiritual–existential crisis, and loss of trust.”7

COVID-19 has presented difficult and untenable working conditions beyond the scope of the challenges frontline health care workers are prepared for professionally. Frontline health care workers have experienced conflict and distress over prioritizing patient care vs their own safety, protecting family members from infection, and the reality that the supplies, medications, and equipment needed to save a life were not always available or were being rationed. Because of high infectivity, morbidity, and mortality associated with the spread of the virus, frontline health care workers were often in the position to be the only person at the bedside at the end of life with patients who were separated from their families. This is not how families should experience the loss of a loved one.4

There is a body of research regarding the long-term effects of moral injury among combat soldiers.3 It is reasonable to expect that feelings of guilt, shame, anger, and self-recrimination stemming from moral injury in these soldiers may be similar to feelings experienced by frontline health care workers during the COVID-19 pandemic and that their experiences increase the risk for acute stress reactions with long-term consequences including increased incidence of depression, anxiety, substance abuse, PTSD, and suicide.4,8 Behavior changes including intrusive memories, avoidance of situations that are reminders of prior events, self-isolation, and potential triggers of traumatic memories are common in individuals suffering from acute stress disorder or PTSD. Additional responses to stress, trauma, and moral injury include disturbed sleep, emotional changes such as numbing, desensitization, depersonalization, and a decreased capacity for empathy and compassion. For some individuals, the consequences of moral injury may be an opportunity for reflection and reprioritization of values and an existential inner process of reflecting on what is important in life.4

Given the consequences of moral injury, it is important for mental health professionals and health care providers treating frontline health care providers to recognize and identify those experiences that have the potential for promoting resilience.9

An analysis of data from 2,579 frontline health care workers in New York City early on in the pandemic showed that key factors predictive of psychological resilience were positive emotions, self-efficacy, purpose in life, strong social support, and not engaging in maladaptive coping strategies (eg, substance abuse).9 Psychological resilience was described by the authors as, “the capacity to adapt and thrive while facing adversity or challenging circumstances,” leading to the question of how can institutions promote psychological resilience in frontline health care workers?9

Initiativespromoting psychological resilience are critical.10,11 Interventions identifying those at high risk for moral injury and in need of support in the form of psychological first-aid and psychotherapy have the potential of improving resilience. Kameno et al administered the short-form of the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale with 4 additional questions, 2 regarding sleep, 1 on appetite changes, and 1 on alcohol misuse, in health care workers during the pandemic.12 The researchers found that women and nurses had higher rates of affective symptoms compared to men and other medical staff, respectively. The researchers noted that early identification and psychotherapy may improve psychological resilience and reduce psychological distress in nurses at high risk for maladaptive coping.12

The need for institutional support, leadership support, education, and training is equally important. Leadership and management are challenged to identify those practices that address the needs of their respective health care workers.10 Survey findings on the expectations and needs of health care workers (physicians, nurses, advanced practice clinicians, residents, and fellows; N=69) during the first week of the pandemic at a single hospital identified the following 5 requests of their organization: hear me, protect me, prepare me, support me, and care for me.13 Management and leadership have the opportunity to promote resilience and show visible support for the health care workforce with unique initiatives to help reduce and mitigate the long-term consequences of moral injury and acute stress response.

Similar to triage protocols and models to meet emergent health care systems demands from unexpected disasters, there is a need for a multilayered mental health care response for frontline workers. Self-care and wellness initiatives have the potential to reduce the long-term consequences of moral injury. Ongoing support, skills training, psychoeducation, and wellness education regarding strategies to address and process the experiences of frontline health care workers are critical for healing the wounds of moral injury. Empathic sensitivity on the part of mental health providers and primary care providers is essential. Listening to “the story” and having the opportunity to process and reflect on the self-talk related to the experience of moral injury can lay the groundwork for healing.

Self-care needs should include the opportunity to seek out and have available a support system of peers and colleagues. All too often the experience of shame, guilt, and self-condemnation are obstacles to seeking self-help and lead to self-isolation. If allowed to process and reflect on those experiences, health care workers may be provided an opportunity for experiential growth and a redefinition of priorities personally and professionally.

Leaders in health care have the opportunity to create and foster a culture of open, nonjudgmental communication. In the face of unpredictable events such as the COVID-19 pandemic, natural disasters, and social and political unrest that impact health care delivery, strategies are available to promote mental health recovery and return to stability and wellness among frontline health care workers.

Catherine R. Judd, MS, PA-C, CAQ-Psy, DFAAPA, is an assistant clinical professor in the Department of Physician Assistant Studies at the School of Health Professions, The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, Texas.

1. Taylor WD, Blackford JU. Mental health treatment for front-line clinicians during and after the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic: a plea to the medical community. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(7):574-575. doi:10.7326/M20-2440

2. Hossain F, Clatty A. Self-care strategies in response to nurses’ moral injury during COVID-19 pandemic. Nurs Ethics. 2021;28(1):23-32. doi:10.1177/0969733020961825

3. Borges LM, Barnes SM, Farnsworth JK, Bahraini NH, Brenner LA. A commentary on moral injury among health care providers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychol Trauma. 2020;12(S1):S138-S140. doi:10.1037/tra0000698

4. Watson P, Norman SB, Maguen S, Hamblen J. Moral injury in health care workers. Accessed January 4, 2021. https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/cooccurring/moral_injury_hcw.asp

5. Shahrour G, Dardas LA. Acute stress disorder, coping self-efficacy and subsequent psychological distress among nurses amid COVID-19. J Nurs Manag. 2020;28(7):1686-1695. doi:10.1111/jonm.13124

6. Lahav Y. Psychological distress related to COVID-19 — The contribution of continuous traumatic stress. J Affect Disord. 2020;277:129-137. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2020.07.141

7. Stovall M, Hansen L, van Ryn M. A critical review: moral injury in nurses in the aftermath of a patient safety incident. J Nurs Scholarsh. 2020;52(3):320-328. doi:10.1111/jnu.12551

8. Pappa S, Ntella V, Giannakas T, Giannakoulis VG, Papoutsi E, Katsaounou P. Prevalence of depression, anxiety, and insomnia among healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Brain Behav Immun. 2020;88:901-907. doi:10.1016/j.bbi.2020.05.026

9. Pietrzak RH, Feingold JH, Feder A, Charney DS, Peccoralo L, Southwick SM, Ripp J. Psychological resilience in frontline health care workers during the acute phase of the COVID-19 pandemic in New York City. J Clin Psychiatry. 2020;82(1):20l13749. doi:10.4088/JCP.20l13749

10. Krystal JH, Alvarado J, Ball SA, et al. Mobilizing an institutional supportive response for healthcare workers and other staff in the context of COVID-19: the Yale experience. Gen Hosp Psychiatry. 2021;68:12-18. doi:10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2020.11.005

11. Park ER, Sylvia LG, Streck JM, et al. Launching a resiliency group program to assist frontline clinicians in meeting the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic: results of a hospital-based systems trial. Gen Hosp Psychiatry. 2021;68:111-112. doi:10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2020.10.005

12. Kameno Y, Hanada A, Asai D, et al. Individual psychotherapy using psychological first aid for frontline nurses at high risk of psychological distress during the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychiatry Clin Neurosci. 2021;75(1):25-27. doi:10.1111/pcn.13170.

#9594. Not Cinnamon: Add A Pinch Of This Warm Spice To French Toast For A Flavor Boost

Warm spices on French toast create a cozy, aromatic breakfast dish that warms your sinuses as much as your tongue. While traditional cinnamon is always a solid choice, cardamom French toast adds new layers of fresh, almost herbal notes for something far more complex and just as compatible with your other favorite seasonings.

Some folks call cardamom the queen of spices — and for good reason. As flavorful as it is versatile, it's a shelf-stable ingredient that lasts a long time, grinds easily into a powder, and seems to taste amazing with just about any sweet recipe you could think of. While it can be a tad on the expensive side, small amounts suffuse your French toast with deep flavor, so even a small jar of seeds can last you quite a while. The key is to mix it with your other dried spices to create a delicate flavor profile similar to mulled drinks, festive winter desserts, and spiced ciders.

Six pods should yield about half a teaspoon of ground spice, enough for roughly six pieces of French toast (though pod sizes vary). Since you want a smooth batter without much texture, it's best to grind the seeds into a fine powder before mixing. The moisture from eggs and milk should help protect the delicate spice, but remember that heat affects the flavor release of spices. Gently toasting the pods beforehand is a great way to bump up the flavor without using more of the pricey ingredient.

Though cardamom has quite a bit of flavor, it's also rather delicate and can slip into the background or be the star of the show, depending on your preferences. In sweet dishes, there are few warm spices it pairs poorly with, and more obscure ingredients can really elevate its flavor for something showstopping.

Just about any warming spice you'd associate with the colder months should pair beautifully with cardamom. Cinnamon is a bold counterpart that can carry most of the flavor profile without overshadowing it when used in moderation. Allspice and cloves are a match made in heaven, providing an almost berry-like warmth to counteract cardamom's cool, herbal notes. Ground or fresh ginger can add a touch of sharpness that offers quite a bit of contrast, providing a similar bite on the tongue to garlic that's far more compatible with sugary bases.

If you really want to bump up the flavor of cardamom, don't stick to just spices. Floral notes from things like dried and ground orange peels, lychee, or guava really round out your French toast without overpowering your spices. These are highly compatible with cardamom and make your breakfast taste almost like a pomander, with an incredible bouquet of aromas the second your bread hits the pan. You can also use food-safe flavoring oils instead, mixing them into your wet ingredients for greater control over how much flavor you're adding.

#9591. The Absolute Best Pizza In Your State

There's probably no food more universally adored among Americans than pizza. Aside from being extremely customizable, every state has its own version of the best pizza — at least 15 distinct varieties and styles of making pizza can be found in the U.S. This makes it difficult to compare them. After all, the differences between a Detroit deep-dish and a chewy New Haven pie are many.

This list sets aside nationwide pizza chains and restaurants that happen to have pizza on the menu, and seeks to highlight the most delicious pizza in each state. We considered customer reviews from all over the internet, as well as any regional or national honors attributed to each pizza, and compared the overall cultural legacy and impact of each restaurant. What we ended up with was delicious pizza places that were worthy of being the best in each state. When a good frozen pizza (or even the best frozen pizzas) won't cut it, these are the spots to check out.

A well-traveled mainstay of Huntsville, Alabama, Valentina's Pizzeria has a reputation for serving New York-style pizza in a deep Southern atmosphere alongside other confections and dishes made in an Italian-American tradition. Joe Carlucci, the maestro behind Valentina's Pizzeria, is a co-founder of the World Pizza Champions organization, and his pizzeria is a local favorite — just check the comments on any of Valentina's Pizzeria's posts.

25783 Huntsville Brownsferry Rd, Madison, AL 35756

People love Moose's Tooth Pub & Pizzeria because it delivers on its goal of offering a "gourmet pizza experience, focusing on creative, quality food in a casual environment." The menu (with a robust list of temporary featured pizzas) reflects a creative urge to innovate. Moose's Tooth is the best-reviewed pizza in Alaska, according to Yelp and Google. There's no shortage of outdoor ambience in Alaska, so in addition to its indoor pub seating, Moose's Tooth offers outdoor, fireside seating for crisp days and nights.

Every pie at Via Della Slice Shop is crafted with artful attention to detail, and it's this skill and the friendly customer service that keep people coming back for more. Though a small and relatively simple operation, the restaurant is dedicated to making pizza of the highest quality; it proofs its dough for at least two days. According to Yelp, the vodka pizza is a particular favorite among returning customers, but Via Della is noted for its rotating flavors.

While DeLuca's Pizza has recently received accolades for its unconventional Spite Burger, it is best known for its brick-oven-baked pizza pies sold out of two locations in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Pizza influencer Dave Portnoy gave DeLuca's pizza an 8.7 out of 10, adding that it "blew [his] socks off [and] can compete with anybody in the country." And the non-influencers love it, too, with some people even driving multiple hours just to get a bite.

Tony's Pizza Napoletana was recognized this year as the No. 5 best pizzeria in the world, according to 50 Top Pizza. Tony's is just as popular with customers as with critics, as it's maintained a high star rating through tens of thousands of eviews on Google. Tony Gemigani — owner and 13-time World Pizza Champion — has spent years perfecting his pies; any West Coast pizza crawl would be incomplete without a visit to Tony's.

1570 Stockton St, San Francisco, CA 94133

Blue Pan Pizza offers delicious, Detroit-style pizza with a little bit of Denver flair. It's known for its Detroit-style pies, but it offers other versions and has been noted by folks for its tasty gluten-free options as well.

Detroit-style pizza is pan-baked pizza, and Blue Pan even serves to-go pies in rectangular, bright blue boxes made to look like its titular bakeware. Blue Pan was voted Readers' Choice for Best Denver Pizzeria by Denver Westword in 2024 and enjoys a huge local following.

A staple of Connecticut and specifically New Haven-style pizza since 1938, Sally's Apizza is a legendary spot amongst locals and pizza fanatics. New Haven-style pizza is made of high-hydration dough and cooked at a high heat in order to achieve a chewy, airy crust.

A new fan of Sally's wrote on Yelp, "It was a perfect meal, in a nice, cozy old school spot, that I'll definitely be craving until I'm back in town."

La Pizzeria Metro is a lovely little pizza place with two Delaware locations that offer a breezy, friendly dining experience and delicious pizza. Customers can even settle at the bar and tables with a view of pizza chefs at work.

La Pizzeria Metro's many specialty pizzas are named after landmark spots in Wilmington, an apt choice given how popular the place is with locals. One local reviewer wrote, "La Pizzeria Metro absolutely nails [creative pizza]. Their pizzas somehow manage to feel both authentic and wildly inventive."

It's no secret online that Florida's pizza options leave much to be desired. But Satchel's Pizza in Gainesville is a diamond in the rough.

It's a beloved destination for locals who praise both its delicious pizza and eclectic atmosphere. Some would even argue it's not just the best pizza in Florida; it might just be the best in the south. Even with thousands of reviews online, Satchel's maintains a very high star average rating.

Antico Pizza Napoletana is a pizzeria located in Atlanta's Little Italia. Founded by Giovanni "Gio" Di Palma, Antico offers only Neapolitan-style pizza cooked in wood-burning ovens, and thanks to its impeccable quality, earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand in 2023. The pizza is so good, in fact, that it earned the highest score out of all pizzerias reviewed in Zagat's first survey of pizza places in major U.S. cities.

Though Pizza Mamo only began selling pies in 2020, it's quickly been established as a neighborhood mainstay in Honolulu and has earned an Ilima Award — Hawaii's most prestigious restaurant recognition. Pizza Mamo's pies are based on a four-day fermented dough that provides a satisfying, chewy consistency in every slice. A local Yelp reviewer wrote, "Best pizza I've had on the island ... the pepperoni has a nice spice to it, and the dough is PERFECT."

Despite its remote location, Embers by the Lake has garnered tons of glowing online reviews – and the pizzeria's gorgeous lakeside backdrop is only a small part of what customers love. A great spot for family outings, Embers by the Lake has earned official recognition determined by customers, entities, and critics, including a local organization called North Idaho Life, which awarded it the first 5-Star Dining Destination Award.

12008 N Woodland Beach Dr, Hauser, ID 83854

Vito and Nick's Pizzeria is known for its Chicago tavern-style pies, which are made with a round, cracker-thin crust and cut into squares. It's a parlor that's been in business for more than 75 years and is an iconic institution to locals and tourists alike. The CBS Chicago Pizza Tournament awarded Vito and Nick's the grand prize in 2023, and the parlor has been positively featured on Food Network's "Diners, Drive-ins and Dives."

Tre Mori is much more than a pizza restaurant — the menu offers finely crafted pasta dishes and baked breads — but the pizza is definitely its signature. Dedicated to an old-style Italian sensibility, Tre Mori utilizes fresh and home-prepared ingredients, as well as supplies and foods imported from Italy (including the beautiful brick oven). On Yelp, Tre Mori is a top-100 US pizza joint, and on Onebite, it earns consistently positive reviews from customers.

8220 E 106th St Suite 200, Indianapolis, IN 46256

Fong's Pizza in Des Moines occupies the same space that once housed the oldest Chinese restaurant in America. As such, it offers a fusion of Chinese flavors and Italian fundamentals. Fong's claims to be the originator of the crab rangoon pizza (Alton Brown swears by it), and the restaurant earns great customer feedback for its fresh ingredients and timely service.

Even though Back Alley Pizza has only been operating for a little over 10 years, it has become a staple of Newton, Kansas, and a magnet for regional recognition. On Yelp, satisfied customers rejoice over the best pizza they've ever had, period. Though Back Alley Pizza doesn't claim a signature "style" of pizza, it does tout its original BBQ pizza as a signature. But you'll be happy with any slice you try.

Miguel's Pizza feels like a well-loved small business with a dedicated following and a commitment to capturing Kentucky's rustic charm in combination with a warm, friendly atmosphere. Pizza Today has featured Miguel's as a must-stop destination, and many recognize the pizzeria as a key element in the economic development of Kentucky's Red River Gorge. All of that is because of the quality of the pizza, which people just can't get enough of.

Zander White, founder of Zee's Pizzeria, pursued pizza-making as a hobby until the COVID-19 pandemic, during which he had to find a new way to support his family. White was so successful selling pies from his kitchen that he opened Zee's Pizzeria, which was named one of the top pizza places in New Orleans by Gambit Weekly. Customers appreciate the thin crust, sweet sauce, and classic taste.

The purveyors at Brickyard Hollow Brewing Company (which began in Yarmouth) realized that few things pair better with a glass of craft beer than a slice of craft pizza, which has become as much of a draw as the beer – if not more so.

Brickyard Hollow has a greater mission to provide fun and comfort to local Maine communities and residents looking to connect more closely with their neighbors. It's received rave reviews from local critics and is rapidly expanding thanks to overwhelming regional support.

In December 2024, Barstool pizza reviewer Dave Portnoy stopped by TinyBrickOven to do a quick slice review. He gave TinyBrickOven's pizza a 7.9/10 rating and $60,000 to turn the small business big. It was that good. TinyBrickOven is a staple of Baltimore, with local customers and other supporters even accepting the owner's self-anointed title, "the Michael Jordan of pizza."

Widely regarded as Boston's oldest operating pizza place, Regina Pizzeria has been serving slices and pies around Boston's North End since 1926. The quality comes from an impeccable dough — chewy yet crisp and perfectly charred — that's baked inside a 900-degree gas-fired oven. Boston Magazine calls it one of the city's best, and in 2018, Tripadvisor named Regina Pizzeria the best in the nation. Taste of Massachusetts included it in its list of top 11 favorite pizzas in the state.

In 2024, Yelp named Loui's Pizza in Hazel Park, Michigan, as the best pizza spot in the Midwest. It's been family-owned since 1977, and for nearly half a century, it's been pumping out top-tier Detroit-style pies that are chewy, crisp, cheesy, and properly sauced. The Detroit Metro Times ranked Loui's as the No. 1 Detroit-style pizza in the area, citing its "tangy sauce, crispy caramelized edges, and an abundance of cheese" as a few of the reasons why this pizza stands out.

When you have the endorsement from global food aficionado Andrew Zimmern, you know you're doing something right. Punch Pizza is the people's pizzeria, a beloved St. Paul institution that has now expanded to 12 locations. It specializes in Neapolitan-style pizza, cooked for about a minute and a half in a scorching-hot, wood-burning oven. It has earned numerous awards and recognitions, including a Quality Business Award in 2025.

Leña Pizza + Bagels is giving Mississippi some long-deserved culinary attention. Chef and owner Marisol Doyle grew up in Mexico, moved to Mississippi, and studied pizza making in Naples, Italy. The restaurant was quickly named one of the best in the United States by both the New York Times and the prestigious Italian pizza review board, 50 Top Pizza. However, the biggest honor came in 2024, when Doyle was named one of the top 100 pizza chefs in the world.

You've heard of New York-, New Haven-, and Detroit-style pizza, but — unless you're from Missouri, you probably aren't familiar with St. Louis-style pies. And Pirrone's Pizzeria, which has been around since 1976, arguably makes the best one in the state. The rectangular dough is crisp and cracker-thin and covered in melted Provel, a triple-blend processed cheese invented in St. Louis.

Eugene's Pizza has remained a community staple for over 60 years. In 2015 and 2016, it was the back-to-back champion of the Montana Mint pizza bracket, and in 2026, Reader's Digest recognized the pizzeria as the best in Montana. Eugene's serves some wild pies, with topping options ranging from taco-seasoned ground beef and sauerkraut to shrimp and mandarin oranges.

Founded in 1919 by World War I veteran Alfonso Orsi, the bakery and pizzeria has racked up thousands of excellent reviews on Google. Its near-perfect score has a lot to do with its pizza dough — prepared fresh in small batches every morning using a simple recipe of yeast, salt, water, and high-gluten wheat flour. Tripadvisor ranks it the top pizzeria in Omaha, and our sister site, Mashed, listed it as the best Italian restaurant in Nebraska.

Red Dwarf is a triumvirate of pleasures: it's a pizzeria, rum-infused Tiki party, and rock show all in one. The Detroit-style pies have a "crispy edge [and an] airy center" and are loaded with topping combinations that include everything from brown sugar-glazed ham, pineapple, and jalapeño to mushrooms, peppers, and garlic creme sauce. In 2025, Red Dwarf won the Reader's Choice Best Pizza Award from Las Vegas Weekly, and commenters on Facebook, Reddit, and Google agree it's the best pizza in town.

1305 Vegas Valley Dr, Las Vegas, NV 89169

In New England, New Haven-style pizza gets all the attention, but venture a few hundred miles north, and you'll find another popular regional variety: Greek-style. With these pies, the dough bakes in a high-walled pan that's generously coated with olive oil to achieve an extra-crisp, almost fried bottom crust. And few places execute it better than New Hampshire's Tilton House of Pizza. It appears on roundups as the best pizza place in New Hampshire and has a near-perfect rating on Google.

New Jersey certainly takes its pizza seriously. Part of that reputation can be attributed to the De Lorenzo family, who opened their first New Jersey restaurant in 1936. In 2021, Food and Wine recognized New Jersey as the best state for pizza in the country, calling out De Lorenzo's specifically as "one of the finest classic pies in the entire Northeast." Its namesake tomato pie is hand-stretched, layered with cheese — then sauce — and baked until charred.

According to the Albuquerque Journal, Pizza Barn is slinging some of the best pies in all of New Mexico. And any pizzeria with a fireplace and a drive-thru deserves special recognition. Pizza Barn is known for its roasted green chiles — a popular condiment throughout the state — which it liberally scatters over its pies and breadsticks.

John's of Bleecker, the famed no-slice pizzeria, has been blazing dough in its coal-fired oven since 1929. The pies are thin, crisp, and beautifully blistered, topped with a just-sweet-enough tomato sauce, and then baked fast and hot. With Google reviewers praising its old-school traditions, service, and the pizza itself, this is one of the most respected New York City pizzerias — if not the world.

Oakwood Pizza Box anchors the pizza scene in the North Carolina Research Triangle. It was awarded Best Pizza in 2026 by Midtown Magazine, a publication that highlights life in the greater Raleigh area. It serves an excellent Northeastern-style pizza: thin, foldable, cheesy, and not overly sauced. Its square pies are about the size of a large pillowcase and can be ordered with a sesame seed crust.

North Dakota has carved out its own style of pizza, which is heartier than your average Neapolitan pie or New York-style slice. Since the early 2000s, Rhombus Guys have been baking doughy, tire-sized pizzas that have earned it the reputation as one of the best (and most inventive) pizzerias in the state. The restaurant's signature T-Rex pizza — a hulking combination of pepperoni, sausage, and other toppings — won the Grand Forks People's Choice competition six years in a row.

Rarely do you see such a consensus on Reddit and Facebook, but when it comes to Il Rione, almost everyone agrees that it makes one of the best pies in Cleveland — if not the state. It serves a gorgeous New York-style pizza that, in 2025, beat out 32 other pizzerias to win the title of Best Pizza in the Land from the local media outlet I'm From Cleveland. It's also a favorite of Iron Chef (and Cleveland native) Michael Symon.

Most of the pizzerias on this list are primarily standalone restaurants. Hideaway is one of the few exceptions, with 27 locations across three states. In 1957, its original location opened in Stillwater, next to the Oklahoma State University campus. With pizza names like Pepperonipalooza and Aporkalypse, it's no surprise that The New York Times listed it as one of 15 of its readers' favorite pizza places from around the world.

At Lovely's Fifty Fifty,  chef/co-owner Sarah Minnick uses her art degree to craft her stunning edible mosaics. Her sourdough starter, local grains, flowers, and seasonal ingredients help her pizza achieve an inimitable tang and toothsome chew. With write-ups in Portland Monthly, a feature in Food & Wine, and an impressive 9.0 score from the Infatuation, Lovely's has become one of the most respected pizzerias in the country.

4039 N Mississippi Ave, Portland, OR 97217

Opened in 1924, the Corropolese Italian Bakery & Deli is most famous for its tomato pie: a sturdy, cake-like dough covered in smooth tomato sauce, sprinkled with a light dusting of Romano cheese, and served at room temperature. Over the century, it has become a cornerstone of Philadelphia food culture, so much so that in 2023, Corropolese's won Herr's second annual #FlavoredbyPhilly contest. The prize? A Herr's chip flavor inspired by its famous tomato pie.

For such a tiny state, Rhode Island has plenty of quality pizzerias, but one that keeps showing up on lists of local favorites is Pasquale's. With a treasured Associazione Vera Pizza Napoletana certification, it's no surprise the pizzeria has earned so many accolades. In 2025, 50 Top Pizza named it the 12th best in the U.S., and Rhode Island Monthly magazine acknowledges it as one of the state's great pizzerias.

59 S County Commons Way, Wakefield, RI 02879

D'Allesandro's Pizza has been making its hand-tossed pizzas since 2006. In 2021, Big Seven Travel named the pizzeria No. 1 in South Carolina. Four years later, D'Allesandro's was one of three pizzerias to win the title of Best Pizza Joint from The Guide to South Carolina. Eater followed suit in 2025, featuring D'Alessandro's on its list of the 13 best stops for pizza in Charleston.

Opened in 1959, Charlie's Pizza House is the oldest pizzeria in South Dakota. Its lineup of eclectic specialty pizzas, with names like "Hepburn's Spicy Delight," "John Wayne's BBQ Style," and "Marilyn's Mermaid Heaven," which is topped with shrimp, crab, and green and black olives, honors Hollywood stars of past decades. The restaurant has also received national acclaim, with the Food Network naming Charlie's South Dakota's best pizza place.

A Dopo is a wood-fired pizzeria in downtown Knoxville that has won over the hearts of residents and college students with its sourdough Neapolitan-style pizzas. The dinner-only pizzeria stepped into the national spotlight after making the list of USA Today's 2025 Restaurants of the Year, and it continues to rack up recognition, most recently receiving a nod from the Michelin Guide in 2026.

Cane Rosso is a pizzeria that has blossomed into nine locations across Texas. Its wood-fired pizzas are all 14 inches and baked in a blazing-hot oven, giving each pie its "signature leopard-spotted crust." Its toppings — beef brisket, bacon marmalade, smoked mozzarella, habanero honey — have a distinct Texas flair. In 2021, Food & Wine named it one of the best pizzerias in Texas, and it has since maintained its reputation for excellence.

The Pie Underground's flagship location, open since 1980, is the most beloved of its dozens of locations — just a stone's throw from the University of Utah campus. Unsurprisingly, its menu reads like it was conceived by the hungry college kids who still love the place, featuring bold concoctions like the "Bacon-Berry Pie," a pizza topped with chicken, bacon, feta, and a strawberry balsamic sauce.

Folino's embodies the ethos of pizza artistry. Its naturally leavened dough uses a 14- year-old starter culture and is cold-proofed for three days to achieve a one-of-a-kind crust that's light, layered, and intentionally tangy. It has expanded to multiple locations throughout Vermont, and it's consistently won Best Pizza Restaurant from Seven Days, an independent weekly newspaper covering Vermont news, politics, food, and culture.

Dr. Ho's describes itself as "the alternative pizza." And we can't help but agree. The pies, each made with hand-tossed dough, include an impressive configuration of toppings like the buffalo chicken with pineapple and pickled jalapeño peppers or the shrimp with homemade basil pesto. Its commitment to innovative combinations, quality ingredients, and sheer quantity makes this one a favorite among Virginians.

The Carlson Block is a destination restaurant, nestled cozily in Wilkeson, a tiny coal-mining town. The Seattle Times featured the pizzeria, asking rhetorically if it's making the best pizza in the state. The pies, pulled charred from the wood-fired oven, glow like an oil painting encased in a rich wooden frame. House-made mozzarella, seasonal ingredients, a deft hand, and a commitment to the craft ensure Carlson Block will remain among the state's best pizza places.

You know what you're getting at Pies & Pints: quality draft beer and fiercely innovative pizzas. Seriously, the pie lineup is extraordinary, with topping combinations like grapes and Gorgonzola, Sriracha shrimp, and Cuban pork with fresh pineapple, jalapeños, and crème fraiche. It's an endless list, which means you'll just have to come back again and again to try them all, as many West Virginia residents have been doing.

Open for over a century, Wells Brothers serves a handful of Italian classics, but it's most famous for its pizzas. In 2026, The Journal Times awarded Wells Brothers the title of Best Pizza and Best Italian Restaurant. The restaurant has amassed thousands of glowing Google reviews, indicating that it may keep serving its beautifully-charred, square-cut pies well into the next century.

A relative newcomer, Bella Fuoco is wowing with its blistered, wood-fired pizzas. The concept started as a food truck, but its brick-and-mortar location has helped chef-owner Brenna Kosowicz bring her pizza to even more hungry Wyomingites. In 2025, Bella Fuoco was formally recognized when the Wyoming Tribune Eagle awarded it Best of the Best in the pizza category.

Determining the "best" pizza is largely subjective. For states with a distinct regional variation, we selected shops that are an excellent representation of that style. We also considered restaurants that have stood the test of time or are pillars of the community, and placed weight on glowing social media reviews and awards. Overall customer experience was also considered, as was the impact on the home state's pizza culture.

#9588. Make A Reuben Upside Down-Style For More Caramelized Flavor

The origins of the Reuben are disputed, with some saying that it was invented in Nebraska while others insist that it is a New York original. Regardless of where you think this iconic sandwich was born, the combination of corned beef, cheese, sauerkraut, and Russian dressing (or Thousand Island dressing) on rye bread is something that few people mess with. The method for making it also tends to remain unchanged, with many restaurants and home cooks pressing it in a sandwich press or skillet. This is just fine for the traditional recipe, but if you want to give your Reuben a layer of caramelized flavor, you're going to need to shake up tradition just a little bit by making it upside down-style. Instead of building your sandwich starting with the bread, start with the cheese touching the pan or baking sheet.

Cheeses like Swiss, which is the preferred kind for making a classic Reuben sandwich recipe, contain proteins and a little bit of sugar in the form of lactose. It's these two elements that react to the direct heat of the pan to create the Maillard reaction, which is when food gets browned, developing complex flavors that make it irresistibly delicious. This contributes to a caramelized note in your sandwich and echoes the toasty notes of the bread. By adding additional cheese between the layers of meat, you ensure that there is a melty element as well. Adding the kraut right before assembling the final product prevents the moisture from getting in the way of browning.

Since the cheese is coming into direct contact with the cooking surface, you're going to need to ensure that it doesn't stick to whatever you're using to make your sandwich. If you're opting to make your Reuben on the stovetop, you're going to want to use a nonstick pan. Make sure it's hot, too, as this can also help prevent food from sticking. You're also going to want to use a thin, wide spatula that you can easily slide between the cheese and the pan to flip your sandwich halves so that you can toast the bread.

If you're choosing to bake your Reuben upside down-style, be sure to use Ina Garten's favorite thing to line a sheet pan: parchment paper, which you can easily peel away from the toasted cheese after flipping your sandwich halves over. You'll also want to ensure you're baking your sandwiches at the right temperature to get both the cheese and bread toasted and crisp, and 375 degrees Fahrenheit is typically ideal.

Regardless of which method you choose, you should always spread some kind of fat on your bread for even more flavor, and this is something you can play around with without breaking from tradition too much. Butter or mayonnaise are typically used in toasted sandwiches, but you can also opt for ghee, which has a nuttier flavor. Bacon fat is also an intensely flavorful alternative, but if you want to mirror the meatiness of the corned beef, go for beef tallow.

#9585. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

Justine Lee is a food writer, recipe developer, and culinary consultant based in New York City. In her free time, she is actively on a hunt for a good almond croissant.
